Mr. Speaker, I understand that last April the scale of relief for pensioners was cut down on the ground that the expenses during the summer months were not as heavy as they

had been in the previous winter. Winter is upon us again. I have before me a communication from Deer Lodge indicating that pensioners on relief are very anxious to have the scale restored to where it was, and also some allowance for clothing. Ordinary work is entirely non-existent, and they carinot possibly subsist under conditions as they now obtain. speakeroldname: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: RELIEF TO PENSIONERS
subtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING READJUSTMENT OF WINTER AND SUMMER ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, from what I heard of the hon. member's question I am inclined to believe that his statement is somewhat inaccurate. I understand that he has inquired as to what the allowance is at the present time.

maintopic: RELIEF TO PENSIONERS
subtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING READJUSTMENT OF WINTER AND SUMMER ALLOWANCES
speechtext: No. I shall repeat my question. I understand that the relief granted to pensioners was cut down last April on the ground that expenses for the summer would not be as great as they had been the previous winter. I have now before me a communication from pensioners at Deer Lodge St. James, Manitoba, in which they urge that the scale be restored to the original rate, and that there should be an allowance for clothing. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: RELIEF TO PENSIONERS
subtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING READJUSTMENT OF WINTER AND SUMMER ALLOWANCES
speechtext: As I stated before, I think the hon. member is inaccurate when he states that the allowance has been cut down. That is hardly a correct way of putting it, because relief has been given during the summer months along lines similar to those adopted in the previous summers. At the present time the rate upon which pensioners receive unemployment relief is figured on the basis of the amount of relief granted by the various municipalities. The amount of pension, plus the amount of relief to pensioners who are in conditions requiring relief amounts to not less than the amount granted by municipalities. That is the principle upon which unemployment relief is now given, and it is proposed that this amount of relief be continued through the winter months.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
subtopic: REPORT OP DELEGATES REPRESENTING CANADIAN GOVERNMENT AT GENEVA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the leader of the opposition asked a question regarding the report of the delegates to the Disarmament conference which I, along with two colleagues and a staff, had the privilege of attending. I have before me two copies of the report in English, with annexes attached. Also I have copies of the covering letter which I sent to the Prime Minister with the report. Further, I have two copies of the report itself in French, along with the covering letter.
The report is rather lengthy. As this can be only an interim report, and as the matter is still very much under discussion it is not proposed at the present time to print it. In the letter which I sent to the Prime Minister I explained to him in a brief way the situation as I understood it, and with your permission I would like to read this letter for the information of the house, as it gives the main points:
Ottawa, November 1, 1932. The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, M.P.,
Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,
I have the honour, as chairman of the Canadian delegation to the Geneva Disarmament conference, to submit the enclosed report on the work of that conference from its opening on February 2, to the adjournment of the first session, July 23, 1932. The work of the first.
session cannot be considered an unqualified success, and yet it is not fair to say that nothing was accomplished. The complexities of the disarmament movement are familiar to every student of the subject. These complexities, which would have made the problem before the conference a difficult one in any case, were increased by several special events, which held back the work of the first session, and which were concerned partly with the situation in the far East, and partly with the exigencies of politics in certain European countries. As a result not as much was accomplished as had been hoped for. An analysis of these accomplishments is given in the concluding section of the enclosed report.
May I outline here, briefly, the progress of events at the first session. The conference opened on February 2, with a general debate in which the representatives of some forty states participated. This occupied almost a month. After the conclusion of the general debate the conference concerned itself with mapping out a plan of procedure for the work before it, not a simple task, and in setting up committees on land, naval, and air armaments, political questions and national defence expenditure. These committees had begun their work before the Easter recess, which lasted until April 11. After this recess the conference concerned itself for some weeks with the question of qualitative disarmament, that is the abolition of certain weapons chosen more particularly because of their aggressive nature, their efficacy against national defence, or their cruelty to the civil population. After a vigorous debate the principle of qualitative disarmament was accepted, and the technical land, naval, and air committees were instructed to examine what armaments might be dealt with under it. This constituted a new and important approach to the problem of disarmament. It was meant to be a supplement to, not a substitute for, quantitative disarmament. It was rightly considered that at this time quantitative disarmament could not be achieved without the prior solution of certain political difficulties. While the representatives of the larger powers were attempting to settle some of these political difficulties, by informal conversations, the consideration of qualitative disarmament went on in the technical committees, but it was not particularly successful. The problem was as political as it was technical, and committees of experts found a technical solution difficult indeed. The result is that the reports on qualitative disarmament finally submitted by the committees to the general commission of the conference are little more than records of their proceedings.
From June 10, when these reports were presented, to June 22, there were important private conversations among the representatives of the great powers in a further effort to find some solution of the more serious political difficulties which stood in the way of progress. It may be said here that these were concerned largely with the German demand for "equality" (that is, the removal of special treaty restrictions) and the French demand for "security." It had become only too apparent that the fate of the conference was contingent to a large extent on the satisfactory settlement of these two questions. While this solution was being sought, a new direction was given to the work of the conference on June 22, by the presentation of what came to be known as the Hoover proposals, which advocated generally a one-third

reduction in armaments. These proposals were debated until July 5, and while there was general acceptance of the principle behind them, it was felt that further time was needed for a consideration of their details. It was decided, therefore, that the conference should adjourn to give time for this consideration. A resolution including all the points on which the governments had been able to reach agreement during the first phase of the conference was then drawn up and submitted for acceptance. This resolution, which is analysed in the penultimate section of the enclosed report, was accepted on July 23 by 41-2, with eight abstentions. Germany and Russia voted against it. The conference then adjourned while making provision for the continuation of the work of the bureau during the adjournment. The bureau, which consists of the president and vice-presidents of the conference, the officers of the general commission, and the chairmen of the important committees, continued its duties during the summer. It supervised the work of a committee on effectives, requested certain of its members to submit reports on various questions raised by the closing resolution, and set up a committee to deal with the question of the trade in and manufacture of arms, a subject which was of special interest to the Canadian delegation, but which had not been reached in the deliberations of the first session of the conference. The main activity of the bureau, however, during the adjournment, has been its efforts to get Germany back into the conference. The German delegate had announced, in voting against the closing resolution, that his government would take no further part in the disarmament conference until the question of "equality" had been settled. The bureau has been making every effort to persuade the German government to reconsider this position. At the same time the United Kingdom government has been also attempting to find a way out of this impasse. It is becoming increasingly clear that unless such a way out is found, the next session of the conference will have small chance of making that further progress which is essential and which the public opinion of the world demands.
The bureau is to meet this week and it will then be decided on what date the next session of the general commission of the conference will be called, when subjects of great importance will be discussed. In addition to the German claim for equality it is probable that the French delegation will submit a scheme guaranteeing that political security on which, in their view, disarmament must depend. The Hoover proposals will also be considered, while the further reduction of naval armaments will also probably be examined. There is reason to believe that, if the views of France and Germany can be reconciled, decisions of far-reaching importance may be taken at the forthcoming session.
The attitude of the Canadian delegation at the first session of the conference may be summed up in the following words: We gave whole-hearted support to any and every constructive proposal for the limitation and reduction of armaments which was laid before the conference. We were at times somewhat impatient at the slowness of the progress which was being made, but at the same time we realized the difficulties that had to be faced and the problems that had to be solved. Those difficulties and those problems were primarily

neither of our making nor for our solution, but it was our duty to do everything we could to assist in the efforts that were being made to bring about some effective limitation and reduction of armaments, as a step in the direction of ensuring world peace.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
George H. Perley.
May I say that there is a French translation of this letter that I am putting on the table.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that explains the position as it existed on the first of this month. Since then, as hon. members of the house have seen in the press, both France and the United Kingdom have put forward somewhat modified suggestions or proposals. They are before the bureau now in session at Geneva, and will receive most careful consideration. And may I explain to the house that the bureau is similar to an executive committee, or committee on arrangements. It has no power to make decisions on questions of policy or principle, without reference to the general commission of the conference, but its reports and recommendations always cariy great weight.
While I am on my feet I would like to be allowed to take advantage of this opportunity to pay tribute to the splendid spirit of cooperation which existed among the Canadian delegates and our advisers at the Disarmament conference. My colleague, Mr. Dupre, Solicitor General, made a definite place for himself among those who were directing the activities of the conference, which was shown in a special manner by his election to the important post of vice-president of the Naval committee.
The other official delegate was Miss Winni-fred Kydd, president of the National Council of Women. There were only two ladies who were full delegates to the Disarmament conference, and we are proud of the fact that one of them was a Canadian. In this way the dominion recognized the fact that the women of Canada have a very direct interest in the question of disarmament. You will not be surprised, Mr. Speaker, to be told that Miss Kydd was a happy and fortunate selection for this place. Her energy and ability are well known, and she was very helpful in every way As for the staff and our advisers, I do not intend to mention them by name but I cannot speak too highly of their capable assistance and of the faithful and efficient service which was given us by them. I can assure the house that we all sincerely appreciated their loyal work. I see

Canadian Policy in Far East
by the press of Saturday that our advisory officer at Geneva, Doctor W. A. Riddell, who has represented the government there for a number of years, was chosen the other day as dean of the diplomatic corps. That is a worthy honour for Doctor Riddell, which reflects credit on the dominion as well.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to add that all of us in Canada are very much alive to the necessity for disarmament as the best way of preventing future wars. We must not be discouraged if this is not accomplished as quickly as we might wish, and we must continue to do everything possible to bring it about.

maintopic: DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
subtopic: REPORT OP DELEGATES REPRESENTING CANADIAN GOVERNMENT AT GENEVA

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext:
On Friday last the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked a question with respect to the eastern situation, his question being in the following terms:
What, if any, is the policy of His Majesty's government in Canada in regard to the situation in the far east and to the Lytton report?
Perhaps I can best serve what I conceive t.o be the public interest by indicating that
Canadian Policy in Far East

it is not thought desirable to enter into a discussion at this time with respect to a matter of this kind, for it not only cannot serve the public interest but would be anticipating action that might be taken, and therefore is to be deprecated. In that regard I have the support of the Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom, Right Hon. Sir John Simon, who in dealing with the same matter on the 10th of this month used these words:
It is the greatest possible mistake to suppose that good is done by individual preliminary declarations.
I think that clearly indicates the position of His Majesty's government in Canada, but in view of the fact that many members of the house are greatly interested in this matter and have been asking questions of members of the government, though not in the house, I think it well to direct attention to a few matters that I trust will make the situation somewhat clearer than it is at the moment to some of them.
First, on December 10, 1931, by a resolution of the council of the League of Nations a committee or commission was set up under the chairmanship of the Earl of Lytton, to study on the spot and to report to the council on any circumstance which, affecting international relations, threatened to disturb peace between China and Japan or the good understanding between them upon which peace depended. Secondly, it will be recalled that a special assembly of the League of Nations was called to consider this matter, and at that session a special committee of nineteen members was set up, much like a committee of this house, to consider the report that would be made. Canada is not a member of the council; Canada is not one of the nineteen countries represented on that special committee.
I next observe that the Lytton report was signed in Pekin on September 4 of this year, and submitted to the council of the League of Nations on the first day of October last. Today the council meets to consider the report. It was originally intended that it should sit at an earlier date, but the Japanese government requested that time be given to enable it to file a memorandum with regard to its attitude towards the report. That memorandum has been filed, and a summary of it was delivered to His Majesty's government in Canada today. There are now two courses open: (a) the council of the League of Nations may proceed to consider the Lytton report, or (b) the special committee of nineteen may proceed to consider the report. In any event ultimately the matter

will reach the assembly, of which Canada is a member, which presumably will not meet this year.
That is the situation at the present moment. If I were to answer the question as to what is the policy of the government with respect to the Lytton report I would be anticipating what will be the attitude of the government after the assembly meets to consider it and gives this important question careful consideration. And as Sir John Simon pointed out, preliminary declarations prior to discussion, or prior to opportunity being afforded to listen to what is being said by others, if carried to its logical end would of course render the meeting of the assembly wholly unnecessary, because every member would then be confronted with a prior declaration -and the whole purpose of the gathering is to afford opportunities for discussion, for conference, for understanding in order that some way out may be found that will result in a permanent peace in that territory.
May I further, just for one moment, direct the attention of the house to the language of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs when speaking on November 10, making' the address he did from which I have extracted the section to which I have referred. He said, in addition to what I have already read:
We shall continue to act, as we have acted throughout, in loyal cooperation with the League of Nations on the whole matter. It is the greatest possible mistake to suppose that good is done by individual preliminary declarations. We shall hope to act, we mean to act, with the League of Nations as a whole, and we have a further ground for satisfaction in knowing that, anxious as this situation is, unsatisfactory >as it is in many respects, we have in this matter been able to act not only side by side with other members of the League of Nations but in the closest cooperation and good faith with the United States of America.
And, as is known, the United States is not a member of the League of Nations. I think that fairly represents in general terms the attitude of His Majesty's government in Canada. But with respect to the whole Manchurian situation, in view of the inquiry, I desire to point out that copies of the report are in the library

I speak from memory, but I think there are four copies-and I believe that additional copies can be secured at the office of the League of Nations in this city. There are, however, a few words at the end of that report, the concluding paragraphs in fact, which I think indicate clearly the magnitude of the problems that are involved:
Manchuria, for a year past, has been given over to strife and turmoil. The population of a large, fertile and rich country has been sub-

Canadian Policy in Far East
jected to conditions of distress such as it has probably never experienced before. The relations between China and Japan are those of war in disguise, and the future is full of anxiety. We have reported the circumstances which have created these conditions. Everyone is fully aware of the gravity of the problem which confronts the League of Nations and of the difficulties of the solution. At the moment of concluding our report, we read in the press two statements by the foreign ministers of China and Japan, from each of which we would extract one point of the utmost importance.
On August 28, Mr. Lo Wen Kan declared at Nanking:
"China is confident that any reasonable proposal for the settlement of the present situation will necessarily be compatible with the letter and spirit of the covenant of the League of Nations and the anti-war pact, and the nine-power treaty, as well as with China's sovereign power, and will also effectively secure a durable peace in the far east."
On August 30, Count Uehida is reported to have declared at Tokyo:
"The government considers the question of Sino-Japanese relations as more important than the question of Manchuria and Mongolia."
The concluding paragraph of the Lytton report reads:
We cannot close our report more appropriately than by reproducing here the thought underlying these two statements: as exactly does it correspond with the evidence we have collected, with our own study of the problem, and consequently with our own convictions, so confident are we that the policy indicated by these declarations, if promptly and effectively applied, could not fail to lead to a satisfactory solution of the Manchurian question in the best interests of the two great countries of the far east and of humanity in general.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext: The other day the Prime Minister said that this matter had not been discussed because it was sub judice. Do I understand that there cannot be a discussion in this parliament until the matter is decided by the council of the League of Nations? I confess I am a little mystified in regard to the relationship that exists.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext:
Our relations to this
matter arise primarily from the fact that we are a member of the League of Nations and we must sit on that report and determine what action shall be taken to give effect or otherwise to the recommendations therein contained. It is an elementary rule that those who sit upon matters in a judicial or deliberative sense should not prejudge the case by antecedent public declarations. They may for the purpose of discussion, talk with one another or negotiate a point of view for the purpose of hearing it controverted by someone else; but the broad general rule is that a matter that is sub judice, that is to say, a matter that is being considered by a body charged with authority as is the League of 53719-87
Nations-the assembly-with quasi-judicial powers, if one examines the covenant carefully, should not be the subject of expressions of opinion publicly which would preclude the possibility of that body being able to treat the whole matter with an open mind, not bound by previous declarations.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext: How can members of the parliament of Canada express their views if -that is the right doctrine?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext: They can always express their views in opposition to the view taken by the government and deprive the government of power.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext: But it would be too late.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext: But as Sir John Simon has pointed out, if you set up any body-for instance, a board of arbitration-to consider a delicate problem in this country, would it be regarded as sound for the house to discuss the problem in all its bearings before the arbitration was held, and to express opinions, one member after another, as to what the arbitrators should decide? That, I submit, is not the true rule, and once we have attorned to the jurisdiction of the League of Nations it must be -taken that we have accepted the principle that -that body is the body to determine and pass upon questions that involve international relations as between Canada and other countries.

maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext: I quite agree with my right hon. friend that this parliament should -not take a definite stand on a matter of this kind. But surely the representatives of Canada, at the League of Nations or at any conference which is going to deal with the matter, are entitled to know what the opinions and views are as a result of discussion in the House of Commons, or otherwise. That is quite different from this house taking, by resolution or otherwise, a definite attitude on the question before it is debated and considered by the League of Nations. The members of this Canadian House of Commons, I submit, are certainly entitled to express what in their opinion their representatives there should bring forward as the views of the Canadian pep ole.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN POLICY IN THE FAR EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even at the risk of asking your indulgence for one moment, I would not suggest at all that the members of the House of Commons might not express any opinion they pleased, but I do say that it is not expedient that it should be done. I say further, beyond (all peradiventure of doubt, that the government should not make

League oj Nations

a declaration of policy, when the policy must needs be to some extent governed by considerations that will arise through discussions that will take place by the tribunal Which ultimately has to decide the matter. It is one of the great difficulties we have, and all nations have, that being so far away from Geneva, although it is true we can now use the telephone, we are unable to know exactly what transpires from hour to hour, having regard to differences of time-and it is sometimes of the utmost importance that we should. Were I to declare to-day an attitude which is in my mind with respect to some of these matters, it might not only become embarrassing but might render the influence of this dominion absolutely useless so far as the problem itself is concerned, for my antecedent judgment would be upon facts which might be varied by reason of concessions made between powers, or by a new attitude being taken with respect to them. Like all other problems of this kind which are dealt with by tribunals other than the parliament of Canada, the representatives of the Countries affected always must accept great responsibilities where they cannot get the fullest possible instructions from their governments. All that can be said is that from the fact that they represent the government, they will, to the extent that it is possible, obtain from the government of the day a clear appreciation of their understanding of the problem and of such modification as may arise by reasons which exist when the problem has to be finally dealt with and which involve, as I have said, negotiations, discussions and sometimes concessions which have to be made by one of the parties to the dispute. Almost any problem is capable of being entirely altered by reason of a changed attitude on the part of those primarily responsible for its solution.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since we are discussing international matters I should like to take this opportunity to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) whether or not he has any information to give as to when and where the international conference will be held. A rumor has appeared in the press that the conference will not be held at all unless and until Great Britain agrees to return to the gold standard.

maintopic: LEAGUE OF NATIONS

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: LEAGUE OF NATIONS
subtopic: OFFICIAL STATUS OF DR. RIDDELL, CANADIAN ADVISORY OFFICER

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: LEAGUE OF NATIONS
subtopic: OFFICIAL STATUS OF DR. RIDDELL, CANADIAN ADVISORY OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an inquiry of the Acting Secretary of State (Sir George Perley) in connection with the recognization which has been accorded to Dr. Riddell at Geneva as the so-called dean of the diplomatic corps. May I say first of all that I would be among the very first to appreciate any recognition given to Dr. Riddell because I believe him to be an excellent officer but I should like to know whether or not the government regards the post which Dr. Riddell holds at Geneva as a diplomatic post. As I understand it, a diplomatic post as considered in international affairs is a post held by one who represents his sovereign and who is accredited by his sovereign to the executive head of some other country. Dr. Riddell's position is that of Canadian advisory officer at the League of Nations; as such it undoubtedly has quasidiplomatic functions but I question very much whether the government's intention is to consider this position as being of a diplomatic character in the sense in which that term is used as, for example, in the case of ministers and ambassadors who are now resident at Geneva and who are members of the diplomatic corps in the strict meaning of that term.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: LEAGUE OF NATIONS
subtopic: OFFICIAL STATUS OF DR. RIDDELL, CANADIAN ADVISORY OFFICER
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman knows
of course that there has been no change in the position of Dr. Riddell and the observations which he has made are absolutely correct. He is not accredited by one sovereign to another as are several representatives in Geneva, he occupies exactly the position which the right hon. gentleman has indicated, namely Canadian advisory officer. In that sense, he is not a diplomatic agent at all.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. M. SUTHERLAND (Minister of [DOT] National Defence):

I shall consider this as
a notice of question by my hon. friend.

maintopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY
speechtext: I have another question to direct to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), whose department, I understand, has charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

maintopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, November 18, consideration in committee of Bill No. 8, respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom -Mr. Bennett.-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.
On article 12.
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake forthwith to constitute the tariff board for which provision is made in the Tariff Board Act, 1931.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
May I ask the
government just when it is intended to appoint this board and if it is possible to indicate the probable personnel?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think the right hon. gentleman would be the first to say that it would be quite impossible to indicate who the probable appointees will be. Last summer
53719-87^
when it became apparent that we would have to consider matters of the character contained in these agreements, the government concluded that it was undesirable to appoint this tariff board until after the economic conference. I can assure the committee that we are endeavouring to obtain the services of men whom we consider will be qualified in every sense to discharge what we conceive to be a very difficult task.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I hope the
Prime Minister will not mind my pointing out to him the fact that since his administration came into office the tariff has been revised several times and is now at a point where I imagine it would not be possible to do very much more by way of an increase. Any real purpose which the tariff board might have served has, I believe, gone by, but I should like to know whether or not the Prime Minister will undertake to say that before further increases are recommended the tariff board will be given an opportunity to consider and report upon such increases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am afraid one could hardly make that promise, for reasons which I am quite certain the right hon. gentleman understands more thoroughly than most. A situation might arise which would require action, as has happened in the past. The right hon. gentleman probably will say that we will still have section 43, but I do not think it is quite apt to suggest that we give an undertaking of this character.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: In the constitution of this board will the Prime Minister be prepared to see that different political views are represented in the personnel? As my right hon. friend is aware, on the board constituted by the United States government to deal with such matters the different political parties are represented. If this board is to be appointed for a term of years it would seem only reasonable that some representation should be given to the different political points of view. I would ask my right hon. friend if he is prepared to consider granting or will grant that form of recognition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman will remember that when the Tariff Board Act was under consideration as a bill, the point to which he now directs attention was referred to by him and other hon. members on that as well as on this side of the house. The United States tariff board is, of course, a much larger one than ours. At the moment our board is composed of three, the chairman and two members. Having regard to the size of this country, as I pointed out
1372	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
when we were dealing with the bill, I am sure it will be desirable to endeavour to secure representation from other than one part of the country, and if it is at all possible, having regard to conditions, to ensure that other than one school of thought, for instance, is represented on the board, we shall do so, but I shall try to avoid purely political considerations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I might draw my right hon. friend's attention to the further fact that under this agreement the character of the tariff board is being altered in one material factor. It is being given a judicial function such as has not hitherto been contemplated. That affords a still further reason why care should be taken in the appointment of the personnel to see that whoever may be selected are at least persons not too biased in their political opinions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I have great hopes that I may be able to secure encomiums from hon. gentlemen opposite on the appointments which will be made.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I hope my right hon.
friend will have better success than was the case in the appointment of the radio board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend would say that.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
knew I had to say it. That is the result of a guilty conscience, I am afraid. Leaving that aside, may I ask whether there will be any necessity of amending the law creating the tariff board for the purpose of meeting the requirements of this agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It is thought and, I believe, correctly, that with this agreement ratified in the form in which it is, the only change that may have to be made in the tariff board will be to provide more ample compensation to whoever may become members of it. That is the real difficulty. May I say this with respect to the radio board: the chairman of that board certainly cannot be charged with being a politician.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am not speaking about that point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The civil servant who was selected for the position is a gentleman who, if he votes at all, has, so far as I know no politics; at least he has not manifested any. The appointment to which the hon. member takes great exception was made from Quebec. It is true the gentleman was interested in political matters but his life has not been lived in a political atmosphere. He was a

professional man of, I think one might say, very high reputation. He was engaged by the present Liberal administration for forestry work. He has had a fine training and career so far as that work is concerned. He has lived much outdoors. He has an excellent education and he is at any rate regarded as a fair-minded man. maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: He was not a cheap man in any sense. He had a fine professional reputation and he was paid large sums of money for the service he rendered. He was highly spoken of by those best able to express an opinion. The fact that he was interested in one election-

speechtext: More than one.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

Well, let us say several

May I say a word on this matter, Mr. Chairman? I realize this has not much to do with the clause at present under discussion, but still I cannot let it go without a word. I have nothing personally against the gentleman. Not only was he a candidate but he was chief organizer of the Conservative party for the Quebec district during many election campaigns. speechtext:
With regard to references to the tariff board, may I direct attention to Hansard of November 15, 1932, at page 1169 with regard to cocoa butter. I have received a letter of protest from a Toronto manufacturer, Mr. J. Wardropper, managing director of Rowntree Company, Limited. This letter, which is dated Toronto 3, November 17, 1932, reads:
I have just received a copy of the record of the House of Commons debate for Tuesday, November 15, 1932, and note from page 1242 of the records that you seized the opportunity to poke fun deservedly at the Prime Minister's suggested ways and means by which he could increase his already large interest in the manufacturing industries of Hull.

How can we get intelligent action upon affairs concerning our industry when such misstatements are made apparently in all seriousness.
May I teach something to the manufacturer of that commodity. There is no "cocoa butter"; there is cacao butter. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I notice that in this article the word "invited" is used, and it is used several times elsewhere throughout the agreement. In the other articles where it has been stated that the government would be invited to do so and so, the interpretation placed upon the phrase has been that the government would do so and so; in other words that it was part of the agreement and that the phrase meant they shall do so and so.
I ask if that is the construction to be placed upon the expression, "shall be invited to vary wherever necessary" and wThether those words are applicable to whatever the tariff board may recommend to (parliament under this particular article.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman is perhaps more fully aware than I am that it is always difficult to choose words which will not indicate that the body to which they are directed is in any sense being coerced, although sometimes it has been suggested that that was so in this case. What happened was that the word "invited" was said by the leading legal member of the British delegation to be the appropriate term to use in a case of this character. I looked it up very hurriedly and was quite satisfied that the word used expressed the proper shade of meaning, when you indicate that a power is conferred to enable a function to be discharged. I think that is as far as I can usefully go in an endeavour to define the term, because the context more or less determines the exact shade of meaning to be given to the word as used. For instance, it might be given a different meaning in one paragraph than it has in another, by reason of surrounding context. In a general way, however, it indicates that power is conferred for the purpose of enabling a function delegated or imposed upon a body to be discharged.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am glad the Prime Minister has given us an interpretation, because the leading legal member of the British delegation to whom he referred, would as I understand it, be the Right Hon. Lord Hailsham. I read the remarks of Lord Hails-ham delivered at Calgary, and it seemed to me they went much farther with respect to the authority which this tariff board will have than the right hon. gentleman is prepared to go at the moment. If I understood them correctly Lord Hailsham's remarks were to the effect that the tariff board would be a judicial body, that its decisions would be more or less binding upon the government of the day and that it would be the duty of the government to see that whatever decision the tariff board gave should be implemented by parliament. I submit any view of that kind

is wholly subversive of the rights of parliament, as we understand them, and as we would wish to maintain them. Certainly those of us on this side of the house would not countenance them for one minute.
As hon. members know there has been an effort time and again, more particularly in the House of Commons, to substitute for parliament in the right of framing a tariff some board which would have judicial or quasi judicial functions. That attitude has been persistently and consistently resisted by the Liberal party whenever it has been proposed in the past. It will be opposed with equal persistence and consistency in the future. We cannot for one moment agree that any tribunal of any character can be established with authority in any way to determine what is to be the tariff of the country, any more than any such tribunal would be permitted to have authority to determine any other tax which should be imposed upon the people of Canada.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I wish to state clearly that so far as the Liberal party is concerned, it is not prepared to place upon this section the interpretation which, if I have read his remarks correctly, Lord Hails-ham has placed upon it. I am not in agreement with Iris view of the obligations imposed upon the government of the day as a result of powers given to the tariff board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, if the right hon. gentleman will be good enough to re-read the paragraph, coupled with the statement of the powers of the tariff board, he will have no difficulty whatever. The tariff board is a fact finding body. I think there was a general agreement in this house and, for that matter, at the conference that we could not substitute for parliament and its powers another body created by it.
I can recall very clearly asking that the Tariff Board Act be carefully read by those who were concerned in its operation, and who were representing the United Kingdom. The Australian act, in a particular and general way will be, if it is not at the moment, clothed with practically similar powers. That may be said with respect to others as well. There is no intention to substitute for the powers of parliament those of a tariff board, it being a fact finding body only. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman may recall that from the discussion which took place in this house I heard Lord Hailsham's speech in Calgary and certainly I did not conclude from it that he had made any statement such as the right 
hon. gentleman has outlined. Perhaps the ex-Minister of Justice, who was also there, will bear me out in my statement. I did not conclude that Lord Hailsham was suggesting that the tariff board was to be substituted for parliament.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Will the facts as found by that tariff board be presented to parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It would appear that the hon. member has not bothered to read the paragraph, because it states that they shall make a report to parliament. It was felt that that was essential so that public opinion might crystallize, if it is thought desirable, in one way or another. Therefore the report is to be laid before parliament.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
Prime Minister if he can tell the house whether or not the proposed tariff board will determine the exact percentage of protection which may be granted to any given industry?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That is a question which I am afraid I cannot answer. That is not the purpose of the tariff board. Its powers are mentioned in the statute, and there is added to it this additional provision, "that such report shall be laid before parliament and parliament shall be invited" to do so and so.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Article 13 states:
Such report shall be laid before parliament and parliament shall be invited to vary wherever necessary the tariff on such commodities.
And so on. In other words, the board will determine whether a tariff should be varied or not. I was wondering whether they could say a percentage would be 10, 15 or 20 as the case might be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It is not a question of
recommendation. They do not recommend to parliament; they make findings of fact.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
They will say whether a
tariff is too high or too low?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
must not place in my mouth words I did not use. I did not say that, and that is not what the act says. The tariff board shall ascertain the facts, as they must be found under the provisions of the Tariff Board Act, and upon that parliament will be invited to take such action as the section indicates.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Then if I may go a little further, its function will be somewhat similar to that of the old tariff board that was in existence until about a year ago?

United Kingdom

speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister a question? Article 13 says that the government of Canada as soon as practicable will cause a review to be made of the duties charged on any commodities specified in such request in accordance with the principles laid down in article 11. Article 11 says:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that during the currency of this agreement the tariff shall be based on the principle that [DOT]protective duties shall not exceed such a level as will give United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition . . .
The question I want to ask is, suppose the tariff board arrives at a conclusion as to what is a proper tariff to give the United Kingdom producer full opportunity of reasonable competition in Canada, is the government in duty bound to put that recommendation into effect?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The section says that
they will be invited to take such action as may be appropriate. The government of the day is not bound by the report, except as to the finding of facts. It will have the report of the board; the extent to which it will be necessary to vary the tariff to effect the purpose is a matter entirely within the discretion of the government.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Does not that bind the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It binds it for one purpose, as I said the other evening, on the principle that protective duties shall not exceed what will give a fair opportunity to the United Kingdom producer to compete with the Canadian producer. Fair opportunity is the basis.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Who is to be the judge of the United Kingdom producer being given a fair opportunity?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The government of the day must assume that responsibility, based upon the finding of facts by the tariff board. I tried to make that abundantly clear; the tariff board is a fact finding body. It reports on facts. Then the government has said that on the statement of facts so found it will apply the protective principle only to the extent of giving reasonable opportunity of fair competition.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Is the tariff board expected to make some recommendation as to whether or not the duties exceed such a level as will give reasonable opportunity for fair competition?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That is not my understanding of what the tariff board is to find. It will find facts and facts only, and on those facts the government has pledged itself that it will act in a given way.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I do not desire to criticize the Prime Minister with regard to his interpretation of the duties of the tariff board, but I think he will admit that from the very circumstances of the case the tariff board is almost obliged to recommend certain action based upon the facts which they have ascertained. Because they will be the only ones who will have the knowledge and information upon which the government can act. The Prime Minister says that the tariff board is only intended to ascertain facts; quite right. But having those facts, who but the board itself can judge what action should be taken?
I do not see how the Minister of Finance or the government, after certain facts have been ascertained by this board, can do other than take them as indicative of a certain rate of tariff. Take for example woollens; in order to give the British producer a fair opportunity in the Canadian market, the board make certain investigations, they must of necessity decide whether 20 or 30 or 40 or 50 per cent protection is sufficient to protect the Canadian industry. I do not see how the board could present those facts to the government in any other form than some sort of, call it recommendation if you like, some sort of suggestion at least as to whether the present or a different rate of duty on these goods is correct. I rather think that the Prime Minister is not quite fair to himself nor to the intention of the government when he says that there will be nothing by way of recommendation by the board. I quite admit that in the final analysis the government and parliament itself will have to come to the decision upon the matter. But I fancy that if this thing is going to be practicable the tariff board, as the only body which can have the necessary information, will make some pretty definite recommendations -you might as well use that word-as to what the rate should be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That is exactly what they should not do.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: How are you going to get out of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Exactly as the law provides. Section 4, subsection 6, reads:
Inquiries under this section shall be conducted in a summary manner in public, except as otherwise expressly provided in this or any other act of the parliament of Canada, and the

respective reports to be made pursuant to its provisions shall succinctly state the facts so ascertained; and each report shall be accompanied by a copy of the evidence, if any, taken, and by a copy of all information obtained in connection with the inquiry.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: What would be the nature of these facts?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The facts brought to the attention of the board by those who ask for change in the existing tariff. Let us be practical about it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Let us imagine a concrete
case. Take the British manufacturers of woollens coming to Canada and making certain requests for reductions; I would like to know just What the tariff board would say to the government. What could they say other than that the tariff is too high or too low, by so much? I do not see how any other intelligent use could be made of the board. If the government does not agree with the board that the tariff should be increased or reduced by so much per cent they will simply not accept its recommendation. But, to be practical about it, I believe that the government is pretty nearly in the position of being obliged to ask that board what the decrease or increase should be. Call it recommendation if you like, I think that is what it amounts to, if you are going to make it work and have any teeth at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The last sentence of the
hon. gentleman contains an expression used so often by hon. members without any regard to what it means.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Which is that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: "Teeth". This is a fact finding body. We are not now considering the tariff act; it was passed last year, after long discussion. But I will deal with the case put by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), the case of a certain type of woollen goods; it is contended by the applicants that the duty is excessive. They then proceed to lay their case before the tariff board, to produce evidence and show what costs of production are, and that the tariff affords more than ample protection to enable their competitors in Canada to maintain efficient production.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Will the board not say, how much more?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Wait a minute. The
Canadian producer proceeds to show his costs of production under efficient management and
fMr. Bennett.]
with efficient machineiy. Then it is for the board to report those facts. It is only a matter of arithmetic for the government to determine w'hat will give equality of opportunity and fair competition. But it is not the board's function to recommend that a certain duty be imposed.
I can however, conceive of a case arising in which they would have to find as a fact what the hon. gentleman suggests. If for instance, the applicant asked that the duty be reduced from 35 to 25 per cent and laid his case on the basis of 25 per cent being ample, the board has then to find whether or not a duty of 25 per cent was ample to meet the requirements of the statute, and if it found as a fact that it was, it would have no right to make a recommendation that the government should reduce the duty; that discretion rests with the administration of the day. But the board finds the facts, and it might in the case which I have just given find as a fact that a given rate of duty was sufficient for the purpose. It will be recalled that when we had the statute itself under consideration I produced half a dozen cases from the files of the American court and showed how they bad prepared and laid their cases, and where the application had been to reduce the duty to a given figure how they had found as a fact that that would be sufficient to effect the purpose they had in mind.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I do not want to carry the
matter further, but I think there is a distinction without a difference. If the board finds that a rate of 25 per cent is sufficient for the purpose required, I imagine that if the government acted upon that finding they would have taken it as a recommendation, whether or not you call it that.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I would like to ask
just how the board are to determine the facts. Supposing two contrary arguments are presented before the board, one by a British cotton manufacturer and the other by a Canadian cotton manufacturer. In order to determine whether the arguments are facts will the board have authority to send men perhaps to England to determine the factors entering into the question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The fact that the tariff
board is to be used as indicated in this agreement does not in any sense add to or detract from its powers. The questions that now are being asked are questions that were asked last year when the bill was under consideration. This is not a discussion as to the merits or demerits of the Tariff Board Act. The

United Kingdom
hon. gentleman must realize that when judges decide questions they do so on the evidence submitted, and that evidence is given under oath. This board is a judicial body charged with the responsibility of determining facts on the evidence submitted by the applicant or, it may be, submitted on the part of others, and the finding of facts, of course, must be predicated upon the evidence which it is the duty of those who use the tribunal to submit to it. That was all discussed when the statute itself was under consideration. This agreement is merely an indication that this body, now existent, is to be used for the purposes indicated.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: If it is found by the tariff board that the duties do exceed such a level as will give United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition, will the government introduce and submit to parliament legislation giving effect to that finding?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That is a matter which
the government must consider.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The tariff board may find as a fact that duties do exceed such a level as will permit United Kingdom producers full opportunity of competition and, if they feel so disposed, the government may pay no attention to that finding of fact at all. Is that what I understand from the right hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
No, neither is that a
correct statement. If the fact sought to be established by the applicant is that a given rate of duty is higher than is necessary to provide for fair competition and equal opportunity, then conceivably the board might find that fact. That is the fact which is reported to the government and to parliament, and the government then undertake to invite parliament to take such action as may be necessary to give effect to the principles mentioned by the hon. member for Provencher in connection with the preceding article.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for North Waterloo is quite right in his submission that in effect there is a finding by the tariff board of the rate of duty which should be charged. It may not be a recommendation ; it is not a recommendation according to the statute. It is a conclusion, but in reading article 11 it seems plain that this article must have been worded in conformity with the Tariff Board Act. Article 11, taken
with article 13, provides in effect that the investigation shall be made as to the relative cost of economical and efficient production. According to section 4 (b), the Tariff Board Act empowers the board to make inquiry as to:

the cost of efficient production in Canada and elsewhere, and what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required to equalize differences in the cost of efficient production.
I submit that what the board does, as the right hon. Prime Minister suggests, is find as a matter of fact what actual duties are necessary to equalize that cost of production. Having done that it seems to me there is not very much left for the government to do but at least bring in the legislation based upon that finding, containing those very figures. So in the end the result is that the tariff board does make a finding at least, if not a recommendation, on which action is taken under article 13; really therefore, it is the tariff board which determines what action shall be taken under that article.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It does seem to me that, without repeating the definition given by the hon. member for North Waterloo, the actual result must be as he has said. What will be the main fact to be ascertained by this tribunal? It must ascertain the percentage of difference which exists between the cost of production in Britain on the one hand and in Canada on the other, and that percentage will be the amount of tariff necessary to equalize the opportunities of both. It does seem to me that the basic and essential fact the board will be called upon to ascertain and determine will be that percentage of difference, which in effect is the rate of tariff necessary to equalize the opportunities of competition. If the government disagrees with that report and says those percentages are not correct, or if it declines to act upon the recommendation even though the percentages are correct, then it seems to me the government must take responsibility for its refusal. So far as action itself is concerned, however, it does seem to me that the fact to be ascertained will be the actual rate of duty which must be put into effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The section of the act to which the hon. member for Shelbume-Yar-mouth referred, and which is being discussed by the hon. member for Red Deer, must be considered in relation to subsection (2) of section 4.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I referred to subsection (b) of section 4.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That has relation to the cost of efficient production in Canada and elsewhere, and what rates of duty are required to equalize those costs. That is one of many factors. Subsection (2) reads:
The board shall make inquiry into any other matter, upon which the minister desires information, in relation to any goods which, if brought into Canada or produced in Canada, are subject to or exempt from duties^ of customs or excise, and shall report to the minister, and the inquiry into any such matter may include inquiry as to the effect which an increase or decrease of the existing rate of duty upon a given commodity might have upon industry or trade, and the extent to which the consumer is protected from exploitation.
That is also part of the same section. I think it is fair to say that if the hon. member for North Waterloo merely means that the tariff board is seized with jurisdiction and power to find as a fact that a 10 per cent increase in duty would effect a certain purpose, or that the application to reduce the duty from 35 per cent to 25 per cent would bring about the result at which the statute aims, that jurisdiction and power clearly are there. I do not think there is any doubt as to that, but I was endeavouring to make clear that this board does not make a recommendation. The hon. member for North Waterloo says it is a distinction without a difference, but I will tell him why that distinction was observed both here and in the United States. It was for the very reason mentioned by the right hon. leader of the opposition, namely so as to not place within the power of this body jurisdiction to recommend a given rate of tariff or duty. They find as a fact that a 20 per cent duty would do so and so, or that a 30 per cent duty would do so and so. Then it is for the government to act upon it, as the hon. gentleman has said; . and we do know that as a matter of fact, in half a dozen cases in the United States, no action was taken.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That is absolutely correct; but it appears to me that article 11 of the agreement does somewhat affect the terms of the general act itself, because it limits the circumference of the work of the board, so to speak, to one point. It is focussed on one point m article 11, and in that it is differentiated from the general act under which the tariff board will be appointed. That one point is the percentage of duty which is intended to do one certain thing and nothing else, namely, to equalize the costs as between the two countries, and it eliminates from review, in dealing with these articles, all other considerations which are found in the Tariff Board Act.
TMr. Ralston.]
It focusses attention upon and confines the duty of the board to the one point, the percentage of difference which may exist between actual costs of production in one country and actual costs in the other, and upon the actual percentage which will equalize these conditions and make for reasonable competition. It does modify the Tariff Board Act itself inasmuch as it eliminates from review all other considerations, and does focus the attention of the tribunal, in this regard, on that one point alone.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Percentage is not mentioned in article 11.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I wish to refer again to a question I brought up the other night in regard to the latter part of the last clause of article 11, which is incorporated as one of the principles referred to in article 13. It is set out in article Id that, although His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that the tariff shall be based on the principle that protective duties shall not exceed such a level as will give United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition on the basis of the relative cost of economical and efficient production, the following proviso shall be operative:
Provided that in the application of such principle special consideration may be given to the case of industries not fully established.
On Friday night I asked the principles on which that special consideration would be given, and although I did not ask by whom, I was given the answer. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said, in reply to my question:
I have already intimated that the test will be applied by the tariff board under the principles clearly set forth in the Tariff Board Act.
Having looked at the Tariff Board Act, and having read article 13, I doubt whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce was correct; I am inclined to think that he was misinformed or misapprehended my question. Is not the special consideration, which is to be given there, special consideration by the government, having regard to the facts found by the tariff board, rather than special consideration by the tariff board itself?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will observe that the principle on which that article is applied is reasonable competition on the basis of the relative cost of economical and efficient production. It will be applied by the board. I should not think it would make much difference in actual practice

United Kingdom
because it would have to be presented to the board in any event whether the industry was firmly established or only a newly established industry. I should think it would not be a very important matter, in a broad and general way, speaking of conditions as they are, but it was put there to protect this situation. I could tell the hon. gentleman of industries -I have not a list of them at the moment- that have come into this country during the last ten years on the tariff as it was.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The silk industry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Silk is one of them, as my hon. friend from Lincoln reminds me.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: You don't suggest it needs more protection?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: No, but it came into the country on the basis of the tariff and was so established. At the time we had a very small investment and now we have millions of dollars, and that proviso was added to the article in question so as to preclude the possibility of bad faith being imputed to parliament when, by reason of the existing tariff arrangement, an industry was established in Which millions of dollars have been invested. An application to loweT duties would be successfully met by the application of the principle that special consideration may be given the case of industries not fully established. The finding of fact would be that this industry had not been fully established and special consideration would therefore be given to it. The government would deal with the facts as found.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I think the special consideration is really given by the government rather than by the tariff board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
As a matter of law, it
would be open to both interpretations.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: But in practice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Well, in practice, in the
first instance, it would be applied by the board and secondly by the government. Both must exercise that power, because the finding of fact would be that this was a new industry and was therefore entitled to special consideration.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
May I point out that
the silk industry was established in Canada quite recently, during the period that the late government was in office. They were the ones that imposed the tariff on artificial silk; they are the people that built up the industry. I just want to call that to the attention of the leader of the opposition.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Can the Prime Minister
tell us when an industry may be said to be fully established?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That question was discussed the other evening and I do not intend to traverse it again; there are rules of the house which would forbid my doing so. It was fully discussed. The hon. gentleman is a great reader, and I might refer him to what John Stuart Mill said on that subject. He would find it much more interesting than any observations I might make and, moreover, he would regard it as much more authoritative.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Would it not be possible for any industry which the tariff board might find to be inefficient to make the plea that it was not fully established?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It would be possible for
the hon. gentleman to contend that he was a strong protectionist. It is always possible to make any contention. Those of us who have listened to the hon. member realize how fully and amply he can develop any suggestion and with what strength of conviction he can express his views.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
But I would not have as
much influence with the government as some of these industries have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I should hope not, for
in one instance we are endeavouring to build up the country, whereas in the other the endeavour is to destroy it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That is a
matter of opinion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Not a bit; it is a matter of fact.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister whether the government will give to Canadian interests the same undertaking that has been given the British government with respect to the right to appear before the tariff board. Article 13 reads in part:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that on the request of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom they will cause a review to be made by the tariff board . . .
As I recollect the provisions of the Tariff Board Act, and what was said at the time that measure was under discussion, the effect was that no matter would be referred to the board, so far as Canada was concerned, except at the instance of the Minister of Finance; in othei words, the discretion rested vith the Minister
