Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
of Finance as to whether an application for review would be passed on to the tariff board. That is quite different from what is being done in relation to British industries. With respect to British industries, this provision makes it mandatory upon the board to have a review of any matters which the British government may request to have reviewed. If I am wrong in that I should like to be so advised.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman realizes, I think that so far as we are concerned we entered into an agreement. It has already been said that duties are highly protective- too high according to the hon. member for Weyburn and o'thers. We say we have made changes in these tariffs ourselves and reduced them, but will leave the matter to be settled by the board; and the government of the country affected, namely, the United Kingdom, will make a request of us. We will honour that request because we have every confidence that it will be made on the sound business principles which govern the requests from one government to another country. It will be recalled that last year when we were discussing this matter the question arose as to the right of audience of those who might desire to be present merely for irritation purposes. This section contemplates information, not irritation and a distinction is made between the requests of a government and the requests of irresponsible parties. I think the right hon. gentleman will realize that when you are dealing with governments you are dealing with bodies which will not needlessly take up time or cause expense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
What the Prime Minister has just said might have come more appropriately from someone who has not so definitely and strongly advocated a Canada first doctrine. I cannot see why Canadian interests should not have equal rights with British interests before the tariff board, whether or not those rights have to be exercised via the British government or by any other route. This section clearly gives to British industries a right which may be denied to Canadian industries or to different classes vitally interested in Canada. For example, should an organization representing the agricultural interests of Canada wish to make application to have certain customs duties reviewed there is no undertaking whatever by the government that its request would ever reach the board. The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada might ask that certain duties should be reviewed-there is no undertaking on the part of the government that the matter so requested would be referred to the board for investigation and report. Such

an undertaking is however, given in connection with requests received from British industries through the British government. This is an unfair discrimination in favour of industries in Great Britain as against our own and in favour of interests in Great Britain as against the interests of the Canadian public and the Canadian consumer.
Might I direct attention to another objection which I have to this section. The article states that when any matter is investigated by the board, they shall deal with it in accordance with the principles laid down in article 11. The study of article 11 makes it pretty clear that the business of the board is to keep the protective principle in the tariff. Article 11 reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that during the currency of this agreement the tariff shall be based on the principle that protective duties shall not exceed such a level as will give . . .
And so on.
I venture to say that any duty which is not absolutely prohibitive will be regarded by parties who so wish to regard it as being in the nature of a competitive duty. If there is a very thin margin between what is completely prohibitive and what is not, that would be considered as permitting competition and thus as bringing the situation within the principle which this board is to maintain with respect to the tariff. The purpose of this article is to give rigidity and fixity to high tariffs, and as such I am strongly opposed to its provisions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The British government makes application to the government of Canada that the board shall deal with an application on behalf of, we will say the woollen industry, to reduce the tariff from one rate to another. The consumer in Canada applies to the Minister of Finance to ask that the board shall consider a certain matter. There is an undertaking in this agreement on the part of the Canadian government that it will refer to the board a request received, not from a British manufacturer, but from the British government. It does not follow that because a British manufacturer asks the British government to do this, the government will. That matter was clearly discussed. The British government has some idea of what is involved in the way of expense and of the serious character of these hearings and the effect they will have upon industry. As far as Canadian applications are concerned, very often they are purely for the purpose of irritation. I use that word deliberately because I happen to know of some of the applications made to the Minister of Finance under my right hon.

United. Kingdom
friend's administration. Some of those applications were made purely for the purpose of causing annoyance. The Minister of Finance must take his chance in this house of refusing or granting an application. The Canada first doctrine applies here if it ever applied anywhere. A Canadian makes his application to his Minister of Finance who is asked in the house, "Did you receive such an application?" He replies, "I did", and he is then asked, "Did you grant it?" He says, "No", and he is then at the bar of public opinion as far as deciding whether or not this government was sound in the position which it took. So far as concerns the procedure in dealing with a government which has made the concession of free entry of the entire products and commodities of this country, manufactured or otherwise, the British government will, first of all, determine whether or not it shall accept the responsibility of sending forward a request from a manufacturer. If it thinks well of that request and makes it with all the responsibilities which are involved, this government will afford an opportunity of a hearing before the board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I should like
to ask one further question in connection with the effect which in practice it will really be possible for the tariff board to give the provisions of this article, having regard to the business generally of a tariff board. The Prime Minister has some knowledge of the length of time it takes to investigate technical matters, particularly where those matters refer to conditions which exist in other parts of the world as well as in Canada. Will it be humanly possible for any tariff board which is appointed to do more than review a very few items in the tariff in the course of a year? Unless it is, this provision becomes largely meaningless as rendering any kind of advantage to those who may seek to have these applications placed before the board for review. There was some discussion recently in connection with what had taken place in the United States under a similar provision in the act governing the tariff board of that country, and a statement was made of an authoritative character to the effect that during the two years the United States tariff commission had been investigating commodities, only seventy-three out of thousands had been investigated. The commission had been working morning, noon and night and that was the sum total of their efforts during two years. Among the articles investigated were pipe-organs, peppers, egg plants and bicycle bells. A careful estimate had shown that if the tariff commission of the United States undertook to complete
its examination of the schedule, it would take until the year 2005. I shall drop the five but, shall venture to say that it will take to the year 2000 for any tariff board to go through our tariff schedule and investigate its items one by one. I believe this clause will be largely meaningless or fruitless in practice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am sure the right hon.
gentleman knows that it is not contemplated that the items in the tariff shall be taken up and investigated one by one. That is the reason why this agreement provides that the request for a hearing shall come from the British government. It is obvious that the British government with its sense of responsibility will limit the requests to matters which it believes to be of such importance as to warrant action being taken. That is the reason why I explained to the house last year that we were limiting applications to those upon which the Minister of Finance would pass. That was provided in the measure under consideration last year, it was provided that it should be a summary application. I venture to suggest that in a single week many, many cases will be disposed of. Once notice is given and application had of the matter to be reviewed, the summary disposal of the matter will narrow things down. If it is so desired, these matters can be dealt with great rapidity. I am bound to say that I do not contemplate the kind of hearing which took place under the former tariff board; I may be wrong, but that is not the sort of thing I contemplate will happen. In any event all this discussion might, I think, properly be said to have been anticipated last year when we were dealing with the tariff board itself, and I have still sufficient confidence to believe that the people who are responsible for making applications will not make them needlessly. The British government will make them carefully and after much consideration and they will be disposed of with great rapidity in a summary manner.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I do not see very much difficulty about articles 11 and 13. I think the cast iron provisions that are contained in the tariff legislation will prevent any board of any kind from at least reducing the tariff very materially. As for the British manufacturer who goes to the British government and convinces them that he has a case against the Canadian industry whereupon they in turn consult with the Canadian government and get the latter to believe they have a case, ths manufacturer will be dead and buried about ten years before there are any results.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
0, ye of little faith!

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I do not think the article will do any harm to anybody; we can depend upon it that it will certainly do no harm to the Canadian manufacturer. He will enjoy for at least five years the duties fixed in the schedule now in force under the agreement. There seems to be a great deal of care taken to protect Canadian manufacturers; they are one group of gentlemen in Canada who to the fullest extent enjoy special privilege by legislation, and every means that can be devised to protect them, whereas those who are not so fortunate as to be engaged in those industries must take their chances. I suppose this will always continue to be so.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I cannot conceive of anybody going to the expense and trouble of carrying a case to the tariff board merely for the sake of irri fating the Minister of Finance. I think the Prime Minister's statement that such was the case deserves a little explanation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: We want to know who did that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Conscience makes cowards of us all.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Conscience does not make cowards of us all. We want to know who is meant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I did not say the Minister of Finance; I said for the purpose of irritation.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The Prime Minister also
said: "Conscience makes cowards of us all." I should like to know who are the cowards. He will not tell us.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I should like to make an observation in connection with the composition of the tariff board. In the House of Commons in Great Britain when this question was being discussed, Mr. J. H. Thomas, Secretary for the Dominions, said that the tariff would be on the basis of raw material, social service, wages, standard of living, capital expenditure and overhead. On Friday we had a great deal of discussion about textiles; much loose talk and suppositious facts and figures were bandied around with respect to wages and working conditions in Great Britain as well as in Canada. In this country we have probably reached a far higher degree of mass production than they have in the old country and when wages in this dominion are being discussed, that fact should be taken into consideration. The thought passes through my mind that this is possibly the first time- and I stand subject to correction-that wages and standards of living will enter into dis-
[Mr. Bennett.J
cussions before the tariff board. Therefore I would suggest to the government that in the composition of this board, the vital factors in the life of this country be considered, such as agriculture, labour. I do not know of any other two great forces in this country more interested in the proper composition of the tariff board unless possibly the consumer and the manufacturer. If this board is going to do the work planned for it, these vital factors should be represented in its personnel.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Carried.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Under protest.
On article 14:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that no_existing duty shall be increased on United Kingdom goods except after an inquiry and the receipt of a report from the tariff board, and in accordance with the facts as found by that body.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: This is asking us to countenance a principle to which, unless the House of Commons is prepared to surrender wholly its control over fiscal policy, it will not submit for a moment. It is quite true the article has been drafted in this case so as to apply to any increase of tariffs, but once the House of Commons has approved the principle of acting only at the instance of a tariff board and in accordance with its recommendations, we shall find that on some other convenient occasion a clause similarly worded will be introduced into the house, and the only difference between it and this article will be that instead of the word "increase" there will be the word "decrease," so we shall then discover we are committed on principle not to decrease any duty of any kind unless first of all the item has been referred to a tariff board and the board has reported upon it. Then we shall be asked to act in accordance with the facts as found by that body. That is a principle with which I do not believe anyone on this side of the house wmuld agree for a moment, and I should be very much amazed if hon. gentlemen opposite would agree to it because it is a thoroughly unsound and untenable position to seek to maintain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I do not think my right hon. friend is too serious about that. Let us look at the matter for a moment. My right hon. friend and the hon. member for Weyburn say that they are opposed to these agreements because they have increased the tariff; they say that tariffs in Canada are so high that even to think of increasing them is impossible. We are saying now that we shall not increase them against Great Britain unless the tariff

United, Kingdom
board finds facts that warrant such action being taken. In other words, we have met the views of hon. gentlemen opposite to the extent of agreeing not to increase tariffs unless an independent tribunal finds facts that warrant such action being taken. The right hon. gentleman is difficult to please. We have endeavoured to please him. Let us not talk about decreases until we have to meet them; we are talking about increases. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. It is very nice to stand up straw men in order to have them knocked down, but they do not serve any purpose in dealing with this agreement. We are dealing with an increase which we say this government will not ask the house to make unless a body created by parliament has found facts that warrant such increase. I am sure, on consideration, the hon. gentlemen will welcome this. It prevents an increase in tariffs without a finding of fact by this tribunal. Everybody, especially on the other side of the house, should welcome it and rejoice and be exceedingly glad that there is to be no increase in the tariff except after an independent body has found facts to warrant it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
While, as my right hon. friend knows, I am not opposed to anything that will help to reduce duties where they should be reduced, I am strongly opposed to the principle of having a tariff regulated by a tariff board, and that is what is at stake in this article. Its application extends away beyond even the various items that are mentioned in schedule E. It applies to all commodities that come from Great Britain to Canada. I can conceive quite readily of an instance where next year, or the year after, for reasons arising out of some change in conditions in this country or to meet some existing need of expense or otherwise we might wish to increase certain duties, even against Great Britain. If we should desire so to do this House of Commons should be perfectly free to act. We should not in any way fetter our rights to deal with the tariff as we think best, in the light of Canadian needs and conditions. The fact that at this moment the article is worded so as to relate only to an increase of duty does not affect the underlying principle one iota. But even if it stood only in relation to an increase, without the possibility of later on being cited as a precedent governing the method of regulating tariffs, I should be opposed to it on the score that, having regard to the changing conditions throughout the world in industry and trade, it is impossible to say whether, two, three or four years hence it might not be desirable
to place some duty for purposes of revenue or otherwise against some particular articles, and even against goods coming from Great Britain. It might be desirable to raise duties in one direction and lower them still more m another. It is perfectly clear that only on the basis of having absolute freedom to deal with the tariff as this House of Commons deems best, and getting as far as possible away from the idea of having tariffs made by some external authority can the house preserve its control over taxation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am sure every hon. member in this committee must be greatly obliged to the right hon. gentleman opposite. He now has established the thesis upon which this government has been operating for two years. He has said conditions may arise in the next year or two, in these days of stress and strain, when it may be necessary to increase duties on goods coming to this country even from Great Britain. It is a most, shall I say, flattering compliment which has been received by the government. I note the loud applause with which the statement is received by the hon. member for Weyburn, and we are all happy to think that there is unanimity in understanding that it might be necessary to increase duties against Great Britain. The only difference between us is this, that in the one instance it would be log rolled, and in the other instance the board finds the facts upon which action is taken. We make it a condition precedent to any action being taken, before raising a tariff against Great Britain, that the facts shall be found by the tariff board. But the right hon. gentleman opposite says that is not the way to do it, that conditions in this country may be such that we may want to raise duties against Great Britain without finding facts at all by a tariff board or anybody else.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The Prime Minister may interpret my remarks in any way he wishes. The text will speak for itself. The difference is between fiscal freedom and the denial of fiscal freedom.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: This section prevents the government increasing any existing duty, but apparently it does not apply to any condition where no duty exists. Therefore a duty could be introduced where one does not now exist. Should it not read that "no duty shall be imposed or increased"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am sure the British government and British people will be greatly obliged to the hon. member, for advocating their rights in this connection.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
And our rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: No, not so much our rights, in that regard. They were content with the provision as it reads, and we are asking parliament to accept their view of it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It is sloppily drawn.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: There is another point to consider. We will suppose the government desires to impose a duty and refers it to the tariff board. Under section 4 (b) of the Tariff Board Act the board brings in a report in which they say, "We believe the duty should be increased by so much." Hon. members on this side of the house oppose the increase, and suggest that the tariff board are wrong in their finding of fact. The government will have the right to say, and will be in the position where they will have to say to the opposition and to the country, "We are sorry; we may agree with you that the tariff should not be increased so greatly, but we are bound by our agreement with the people in the United Kingdom to increase this tariff in accordance with the finding of the tariff board."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That is not according to the facts at all.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The facts found are:
What increase or decreases in rates of duty are required to equalize differences in the cost of efficient production.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That is only one of
several.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That is one which will be found. If the tariff board finds what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required to equalize differences in the cost of efficient production, then I say, by reason of the agreement with our friends in the United Kingdom, we are bound hand and foot to the findings of the tariff board, and we simply must act as a rubber stamp.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I suggest my criticism of the government is the very opposite from that attributed by the Prime Minister to the leader of the opposition. I put it in a very safe and careful manner. speechtext:
I fancy from the looks on the faces of some of the hon. gentlemen's colleagues that they have anticipated the answer. maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

I find nothing in the

speechtext: What value is the right of audience to the British producer if when he has had his audience and established his case the facts as found are not to be acted on by the government?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

Exactly the same right as the cement producers had before the late tariff board. That I think will be a con-

It may follow that the plaintiff wins, who has a very poor lawyer, and the defendant, who has a good lawyer, loses. The right of audience is the right to present your case just as you please. The judgment of the court will depend upon its appreciation of the evidence. The action of the government will be governed by two factors; first the government's general policy, and second, public opinion. By reason of the laying on this table of the proceedings, and findings of fact by the board it will be influenced by public opinion outside the house and public opinion within.

I am much obliged to

speechtext:
The Prime Minister has given a perfect example, I think, of how remarks may be misinterpreted merely by the inflection of the voice. When I asked whether that would be keeping faith I was voicing exactly the argument set forth by the Prime Minister early in the discussion of this agreement. There were certain points which perhaps were not clearly set out in the agreement, and the right hon. Prime Minister made something of a fuss, if I may use the word, in stating that the government had conducted these negotiations with the British government in good faith, and that if everything was not absolutely covered he knew the British government would keep faith, just as this government would. Now when we talk about the ascertain-
53719-88J
ing of facts-and the discussion had turned pretty much on that phrase-I will say this: While parliament must keep absolutely within its own control the changing of tariffs, whether up or down, I do say that unless there is some very special reason why they should not do so, the government should act according to the suggestion or recommendations, if you like, of the tariff board which has ascertained those facts. If, except for some very good reason, the government do not act upon those facts so ascertained, they will not be keeping faith no matter what the Prime Minister says. He referred to those words and gave a peculiar intonation to a more or less impromptu remark of my own. I do not want to have those words construed by my right hon. friend or anyone else as suggesting for one moment that there is any breach of faith on the part of the government.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think the Prime
Minister will agree that with regard to articles 13, 14 and 15 the agreement is perhaps a little obscure. That is what has led to some of the differences with regard to the right of audience. I think I have the meaning; I think article 13 refers to cases in which the British government itself may initiate a review of the duties on commodities which they may specify. They may ask for a review to find out whether or not the principle set out in article 11, that is, that there shall be an equality of opportunity, is being lived up to. The next section is entirely different. As I understand it, the British government do not institute the hearing before the tariff board. That is instituted by the Canadian government itself or by someone applying for a change in the duty. Then there is a provision to the effect that the British producers who are interested may appear before the board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That applies to both sections.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am referring only to the initiation of the hearing. Under article 13 the British government initiates the review, and I take it that only through the instrumentality of the British government would a producer have the right to appear. Under article 14 the Canadian government, or someone in Canada, initiates the review and asks for a change in the duty, in which case there is no intervention whatever by the British government, so far as I can see. Under section 15, however, the British producer is entitled to an audience.
Coming back to the words of the Prime Minister a little while ago I submit that this is an infraction of the principle he has laid

down. He says the reason for it is that the British have paid for this right of audience by giving us what has been given in the agreement.

speechtext: And they have a direct interest in it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I cannot conceive how their interest would be more direct now than it was before. Just as it was before, the duty is still being imposed against those goods. However, the Prime Minister says they have purchased that right of audience, and I take his word and leave him to be judged as to that distinction. But this does give the right of audience direct to the British producer, without regard to the intervention of the British government. The moment the British producer learns that an application is being made before the tariff board he may exercise his right to be heard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
My memory of the
discussion with regard to that article is this: Obviously the British government could not be represented before the tariff board as such, but the producers, being the (people affected, would be able to be represented. The provision is to remove all doubt as to their right to be there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It seems to me that the really important point in connection with this article is what it is expected to secure to the British interests which are to have the right to appear. Perhaps at this point more appropriately than at any other I can refer more specifically to what Lord Hailsham said in Calgary. I did not have the opportunity to hear Lord Hailsham, as my right hon. friend and the ex-Minister of Justice did, but his address was published in full in the Fortnightly Law Journal of September 15, 1932. At page 67 of that journal I find the following paragraph, which deals with Lord Hailsham's conception of the powers of this tariff board and the obligations which it places on the government and the parliament of Canada:
... in the dominions a tariff tribunal shall determine what is necessary to afford protection in accordance with these principles, and the government undertakes to take the necessary steps to give effect to its findings of fact. I think a lawyer above all ought to be able to appreciate the importance of ensuring that there shall be an impartial investigation and a decision on facts, and I think the politician ought to be able to appreciate the importance of taking the tariff as far as possible out of polities. It may be said that these provisions leave the whole efficiency of our principles to the mercy of a tribunal, and that is true. It is no good having good laws unless you have an efficient and reliable tribunal to administer

them, but ladies and gentlemen, I believe it to be true that one of the greatest assets of the British commonwealth of nations is the impartiality and high standing of the tribunals, and I believe that there is nothing which has helped more to establish the reputation of British justice and British freedom throughout the world than the confidence which every man feels in the fairness of the tribunals and the fairness of the decisions which they render, and I can imagine nothing which is better calculated to ensure the success of the principles which I have enunciated than the knowledge that a Canadian tribunal in Canada is impartially to investigate the facts and a Canadian government is going to be the government which is going to give effect to the findings of fact.
That, Mr. Chairman, is simply a statement that so far as this tariff board is concerned, to all intents and purposes it is to be a judicial body, similar to the supreme court or any court in the land. It is to give decisions based on the facts, and the government are obligated to carry out those decisions. What ever we may say with regard to the duties of the courts in deciding matters which come before them, whether they be matters of civil right or criminal matters we must admit that the field of the judiciary in relation to the administration of the law is one thing, while the field of parliament in relation to the making of laws is quite another and fundamentally different one. Any interpretation which involves a surrender, as this interpretation does, of the rights of parliament to a board which is to be a judicial body, and which is to say what customs duties shall or shall not be imposed, runs wholly counter to the fundamental principles governing the imposition of customs duties and other forms of taxation as stated this afternoon by the Prime Minister as well as by those on this side of the house. So long as we are in agreement that this parliament is perfectly free to do as it pleases with duties where they refer to matters that have been submitted to the board and is not, as Lord Hailsham says, obligated to carry out any decisions of the board, I have nothing further to say; but I think it is very important that the people in Great Britain as well as in this country should realize that one interpretation is being placed upon this section by Lord Hailsham in England while another and quite different interpretation is being given it by the Canadian parliament.

speechtext:
A few moment ago the Prime Minister said, "We have formed this body," meaning the tariff board. I would point out that the board has not yet been formed. About the first act that this government did after coming into power was to scrap the tariff board which had functioned under

United Kingdom
the late administration, and hon. gentlemen opposite said that they were going to institute a new tariff board that would be a tariff board, in the words of the Prime Minister. Yet they have waited, from 1930 up to the present time, without forming the board, and now at this late date the Prime Minister stands up in this house and says, " We have formed this body I repeat, they have not formed it yet. May I ask the Prime Minister now a question which I put to the Minister of Trade and Commerce last Friday when one of the tariff items was under consideration: Why has the government waited all this time without forming the tariff board? Why did they not form it so that it might review all these questions of the tariff, as between Canada and the United Kingdom, prior to the conference? It is only camouflage, and they are prolonging matters to help their friends who are in favour of high tariffs. I would ask the Prime Minister in all seriousness: Why has he delayed forming this tariff board, or advisory tariff board, or whatever he calls it, until this late date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The hon. member was not in the house this afternoon or he would have heard the whole story at length. I do not think it is necessary to repeat it beyond saying that the tariff advisory board under the late administration was formed by order in council for which there was no sanction by statute, and the chairman of the board having resigned and having been elected to parliament, that terminated it. In order to make it perfectly clear, however, steps were taken by order in council to rescind the order in council under which the body had functioned. We said that it should be by statute and we passed a statute in 193d. The appointments have not been made. The reasons why the tariff was dealt with as it was in 1930 and 1931 have been given so frequently that it is not desirable to take up the time of the committee today going over them again. But I would put this question to the committee. What would be the sense of endeavouring to answer a question when the hon. gentleman who puts the question answers it himself by saying, "This is camouflage to protect the manufacturers of the country "? When you ask a question and answer it yourself what is the purpose of asking someone else to answer it? It shows perfectly clearly that there is no intention to accept any answer as relevant to the question asked. This is camouflage to protect your friends, says the
hon. gentleman. Well, since he makes that statement in answer to his own question, I do not see that any further observations are necessary.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: With all due deference to the Prime Minister, I submit that he has not answered my question at all. I would say that the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman in the last two or three minutes were camouflage pure and simple.

On article 16:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that customs administration in Canada shall be governed by such general principles as will ensure: (a) the avoidance, so far as reasonably possible, of uncertainty as to the amount of customs duties and other fiscal imposts payable on the arrival of goods in Canada; (b) the reduction of delay and friction to a minimum; and (c) the provision of machinery for the prompt and impartial settlement of disputes in matters appertaining to the application of tariffs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: This agreement was signed on August 20. Can the Prime Minister tell us what if anything has been done since the agreement was signed to carry out the undertaking of this article?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
On October 6 the House of Commons was called together. On the 12th the agreements were submitted to the House of Commons. It is now the 21st day of November and the agreements have not yet been passed. In Great Britain they have been passed, and in Australia the same action has been taken. We have done all we could to enable this to become law, but up to the moment it is not. The only thing that is law is the schedules, because under our practice they become effective. But our efforts to get the agreement through have not been crowned with success, judging by Hansard. "So far as reasonably possible, of uncertainty as to the amount of customs duties and other fiscal imposts payable on the arrival of goods in Canada": that is a matter of administration. Complaints were made by British importers that there were difficulties which they experienced and which should be overcome. I think it is only fair to say that from the day the agreement was signed, and prior to its being signed, all the officials of the customs department have been endeavouring by every means in their power to make easier and simpler, and less subject to criticism, the passing of entries through customs. We all admit that conditions have made them extremely difficult. When I explained our diffi*
1390	COMMONS
Imperial Conjerence-Trade Agreements
culties to the British delegation and their permanent officials, I am bound to say that they took a much more reasonable view of the matter than previously. Here we are on the northern half of a continent beside 122 millions of people. We are endeavouring to maintain our integrity, financial, industrial and otherwise, and it is a task that tries men as perhaps few tasks have tried them. In administration there are difficulties by reason of exchange. That is the primary difficulty. There are difficulties between the United States and Canada because of exchange differences, and they are very acute because they vary from day to day. To formulate rules that would govern is not easy. Then there are difficulties of exchange with every other country with which we do business, and that has added greatly to our burden. What we have been endeavouring to do, what the minister and all his officials have been doing, is to avoid, so far as reasonably possible, uncertainty as to the amount of customs duties and other fiscal imposts payable on the arrival of goods in Canada. It was contended, quite improperly-at any rate investigations which I have personally made would seem to indicate that the contention was not warranted -that one did not know what duty would be paid on goods because we fixed a value for duty on goods that might be imported from Great Britain. It will be observed that we have already passed a statute that gives effect to the contention, which we conceded, that we should remove that clause so far as it affects British goods.

speechtext: I do not think it is passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It stands for third reading; it is still before the house. We have passed it through committee and it now stands for third reading. That statute, we believe, will meet that difficulty. "The reduction of delay and friction to a minimum": The causes of delay in connection with the passing of entries are not always attributable to governments, but an effort is being made to overcome that difficulty by instructions from the Commissioner of Customs. Since the conference, I have asked for suggestions from those who have had great concern in the conduct of our customs, and the department has been endeavouring to meet the situation. The minister can speak more freely of that than I can. "The provision of machinery for the prompt and impartial settlement of disputes in matters appertaining to the appli-

cation of tariffs": We believe that the provision made last year in the tariff aot, to which attention may be directed, in part 2 of chapter 55, will meet the situation:
From and after a date to be fixed by the governor in council, all the powers, functions and duties of the board of customs shall be assigned to and be transacted by the tariff board constituted by this act.
Before this government or its predecessor came into office it had been the practice to have practically the same body pass in review on appeal upon the facts which it had determined in the first instance. I dare say the right hon. gentleman recalls that protests were made from time to time. The board of customs was dominated to a large extent, not necessarily by numbers, by those from whose decisions appeals were made. The committee will recall that last year I made the suggestions which are now embodied in the Tariff Board Act with a view to getting a tribunal which could not in any sense be connected with government as the court of appeal in connection with administration.
I have been told, and I am only passing on what I have received by way of information, that the Customs Act is the most difficult act we have to administer. Everyone knows the difficulties in connection with putting through entries. There is the question of checking up invoices and other matters. Since this agreement was signed the commissioner has endeavoured to meet the situation by ascertaining the date of arrival of large shipments and advising consignees that they should be prepared to furnish evidence as to the exact cost in the country of origin. I recall the other day that I had to pass a customs entry when coming in from the United States. I had purchased a piece of antique silver and the difficulty I experienced in passing this article was considerable. There was the question of establishing the value in the country of origin; the question of the value of the money of the country of origin converted into our money; the question of the surcharge of three per cent; the question of our sales tax, which is a domestic tax, and the question of the ordinary customs tariff. When you combine all these they look quite formidable. The department has settled upon a form of invoice to be used by those who ship into this country, and every effort is being made and will be made to reduce the friction which arises because of abnormal conditions. We are now endeavouring to provide in this tariff board a tribunal to which appeals can be taken summarily and disposed of quickly.

United Kingdom
Mr, MACKENZIE KING: I do not believe anyone will take exception to this article; in fact, I commend the government for including it in the agreement. The only criticism I have to make is that all these things which are of any assistance or value to the country generally seem to come only at the instance of requests made by Great Britain or parties there instead of in response to the demands of our own people. If there is one matter above another about which Canadian importers have been complaining ever since the present administration came into office, it is the manner in which the tariff is being administered. Notwithstanding what the duties may be, the rulings, valuations and technicalities of one kind or another are such as to make it almost impossible to bring into this country articles from any other part of the world. If these principles are sound with regard to commodities coming from Great Britain, they are equally sound with regard to commodities coming from other parts of the world. I hope the government is ready to tell us that it is prepared to carry out the same principles in administering the tariff with respect to commodities coming into Canada, irrespective of the country from which they come. If these principles are sound, they should be applied generally; if they are not sound, they should not be invoked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The observations of the light hon. gentleman are perfectly fair and his criticism is not unwarranted. There has been great difficulty in administering the Customs Act and the tariff because of the conditions to which I have referred. The fact that this article is in this agreement might be open to objection; when it was put there I quite appreciated that it would be said that this should not be necessary. As a matter of fact, it is not necessary that it should be there at all. I should like to demonstrate to hon. members the difficulties which this country is experiencing in connection with the administration of a statute like the Customs Act under the present abnormal conditions. I have seen importers on more than one occasion. Shortly after England went off the gold standard the question of the value of the pound sterling became important and I should like to give an illustration of how this worked out. Our tariff is based on the pound sterling being worth $4.86. Let us take an item valued at a pound and bearing a duty of twenty-five per cent. The duty would amount to about 81.22, disregarding the fraction. That amount added to $4.86 makes 86.08 as the total value ol the article and the duty. The pound sinks to $3.80, twenty-five per cent of that would
be 95 cents, which gives a total of S4.75 or 11 cents less than the face value of the pound upon which our duty rate has been predicated, not only by this government but by all governments since confederation. These importers interviewed me and I told them that the following two weeks should demonstrate the effect of England's going off the gold standard upon the value of commodities. It was expected that wages and commodity values would rise. I told them to come back in about two weeks, that in the interval I would watch the operations of trade and commerce and they could do the same. They came back and they told me that the prices of commodities had not risen as rapidly as was expected, nor had wages increased. It is a singular Jhing, but the fact is that the expectations in Great Britain in that regard were not met. Trade figures which were produced at the time of the conference showed that the increase in the prices of commodities was about S.8 per cent. I then suggested to these gentlemen that we should fix the value of the pound for our purposes at $4.40 or substantially 10 per cent less than the par value upon w'hieh our tariff had been ranged. Instead of $4.86, we made it $4.40, which made a reduction in value for our purposes of 46 cents. We did not make this law in its entirety, we found it on the statute books.
When it came to dealing with what has been called the dump duty, mentioned in the next article in this agreement, I explained to the members of the delegation from the United Kingdom and elsewhere that we were confronted with this situation: if we left the pound at $4.40 instead of $4.86, its value would be reduced by ten per cent compared with the original value; it was then suggested that we would establish a fifteen day average for the real value, and the difference between the real value, which might be $3.80, and $4.40 would represent what has been incorrectly termed a currency dump duty. That is one of the problems with which this government had to deal. It is an administration problem but it makes for friction and difficulty. If you have a pound fluctuating from day to day it becomes almost impossible to carry on. As I have said, what we did wTas to establish a fifteen day average value, in other words, we arrived at a value twice a month. We made $4.40 instead of $4.86 the par value of the pound for the purposes of these computations. The effect of this upon my illustration would be that you would have $4.40 with a twenty-five per cent duty of SI.10. That would make the value of the commodity plus the duty, $5.50 as against $6.08, w7hich was the figure
1392	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
parliament had in mind when it imposed the duty. Many of those duties were imposed by parliament when Mr. Fielding was Minister of Finance. I point out these matters because they were in the minds of the British delegates; their merchants were complaining. I discussed the matter with them at some length. The Minister of National Revenue was on a committee with them; they brought in a large number of recommendations and we explained to them our difficulty. Finally we said; We are quite content to put in this document an article whereby we shall do our very best to meet the situation. It is of some value to British producers because we are doing our best in respect to them. As the right hon. gentleman has suggested, if it accrues to the benefit of Great Britain, it of course accrue? to the benefit of all, because the Customs Act cannot be administered in one way in respect of one set of importers and in a different way in respect to another. That is the whole position and is the reason for this article being in this agreement.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
No, but when our
British- preferential tariffs were being made, they were based upon the par value of the pound. I think the hon. gentleman will have no difficulty in verifying that from those who were nearest to Mr. Fielding in the preparation of those tariffs.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
My point is that it is
only this government-perhaps I am wrong and when the committee resumes, we shall know for sure-that has ever adopted the principle of giving a fixed or arbitrary value to the pound. That is to say, we have accepted, generally speaking, the current exchange value of the currency of the country of origin and have charged our duty at so much per cent based on the number of Canadian dollars represented by that currency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
All I can say is this,
that after we had discussed this matter pro and con, the representative here of the British authorities stated, not privately, that we had

done what he conceived to be a very fair thing under the circumstances, because we could have operated in a way that would have been vastly more difficult from the standpoint of those concerned.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
My point is that it is not a representative of the British government about whom we are talking. We are talking about what I think is an arbitrary increase in the cost of goods to the people of this country, brought about by a value of $4.86f being given to the pound when it was only $4.40 or say $4.40 and the government not only figuring on a basis of $4.86| but adding to that the difference between the pound at an arbitrary value of $4.40 and the current rate. That is something with which it seems to me the representative of the British government would not have very much to do, but it essentially affects not only the Canadian consumer but the Canadian importer. Nothing has been more marked in the last two years than the uncertainty suffered by business, which uncertainty has been caused by this variable rating of the pound from time to time. That is the thing of which importers and consumers complain, and it is in regard to that that I, for one, welcome the insertion in this agreement of the particular provision which appears. As my right hon. leader has intimated, it is I think humiliating to Canada to find that this is brought about by the intervention of the British government and of British representatives when for two years there has been an outcry in this country and in this house with regard to the uncertainty which exists respecting importations and the very arbitrary amounts which are being imposed on importations of goods particularly from Great Britain.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
We are on article 16.
Article 16 agreed to.
On article 17:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that all existing surcharges on imports from the United Kingdom shall be completely abolished as soon as the finances of Canada will allow. They further undertake to give sympathetic consideration to the possibility of reducing and ultimately abolishing the exchange dumping duty in so far as it applies to imports from the United Kingdom.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister, or the min-

United Kingdom
ister in charge, concerning existing surcharges. Does this article refer particularly to the three per cent excise tax and is that the surcharge to which the provision refers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: So far as I am aware that is all to which it refers. That is the only one I had in mind at the time.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
In my view the
expression "shall be completely abolished as soon as the finances of Canada will allow" is rather indefinite. I suppose the government of Canada will be the judge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It is not very hopeful for just a little while?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: No.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister tell us anything more than is indicated by the article with regard to the prospect of "sympathetic consideration," so far as the abolition of the exchange dumping duty is conoemed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member does not desire to prolong this discussion beyond what may be useful. Everything that can be has been said with respect to the point he raises. The world economic conference, if it comes into being, may be able to solve the problem. As it stands, the hon. member is fully aware of the circumstances, and I have nothing to add to what I have said.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I w'as speaking only of the exchange dumping duty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I understand that.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman consider the world economic conference will have any effect on that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I say it is a very important factor in determining what shall be done about it. As matters stand to-day, with prices and exchange as they are, it is unnecessary to remind hon. gentlemen that the fluctuations make the transaction of business extremely difficult and that some stabilized form of exchange is very desirable, and will doubtless be accomplished in time.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is right when he states that we do not wish to prolong this discussion. I would point out however that the United States is in exactly the same position as we are, so far as fluctuation is concerned, and as I understand it the exchange dumping duty is not in operation
there. It seems to me therefore that in view of the undertaking given in this article, the Prime Minister might well consider the abolition of the exchange dumping duty without waiting for the world economic conference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: If, with safety to the body politic, it could have been done, it would have been done. In our opinion it could not be done, and it will not be done until it is considered safe for Canada to do it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: What does the Prime Minister mean by "safe"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: So as not to destroy the country by creating a chaotic condition.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Doesn't the Prime Minister think the finances of the country would be improved if the government were to allow the goods to come in, and collect duty on them? No answer.
Article 17 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Articles 18 and 19 have already been agreed to. We now turn to article 20.
On article 20:
Nothing in this agreement shall prejudice or diminish any of the benefits enjoyed by any of the parties thereto under the Canada-West Indies Trade Agreement dated the 6th of July, 1925.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Article agreed to.
On article 21:
This agreement is made on the express condition that, if either government is satisfied that any preferences hereby granted in respect of any particular class of commodities are likely to be frustrated in whole or in part by reason of the creation or maintenance directly or indirectly of prices for such class of commodities through State action on the part of any foreign country, that government hereby declares that it will exercise the powers which it now has or will hereafter take to prohibit the entry from such foreign country directly or indirectly of such commodities into its country for such time as may be necessary to make effective and to maintain the preferences hereby granted by it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister state, having regard to this article, the significance of the renunciation or breaking off of the trade agreement between Russia and Great Britain?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will recall that a commercial treaty was being negotiated between Great Britain and Russia by Mr. Arthur Henderson and soviet authorities. Difficulties were experienced in completing the treaty along the lines suggested, and a protocol was signed which had the effect

of a temporary treaty. It was provided in the protocol that it might be terminated on six months' notice, and inasmuch as the terms of the treaty would be to prevent this section becoming operative, as by its terms provided, the British delegation undertook to give notice within the terms of the protocol. Such notice was given and is now running. The effect of course is that they are then free, beyond question, to give effect to this article of the agreement. Without renunciation of the agreement it is a matter of extreme doubt ' whether or not there would be any power on the part of the government of the United Kingdom to give effect to the conditions of the article, in the event of its being necessary to do so.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has not before him the term of the treaty which might nullify the effect of article 21?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I did not think it necessary to bring it, but if I remember correctly the protocol did not specify the term, because it provided for the negotiation of a treaty at an early date. The express provision was that it should remain in effect until the expiration of six months' notice by either party. If the hon. member is particularly interested I shall have the information for him tomorrow.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: No. I wanted to know the effect of whatever term there may have been in the treaty which would nullify article 21. There might quite possibly be a treaty and still nothing in it

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Oh, I understand the hon. member now. The most favoured nation clause was in the treaty.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Was given to Russia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Yes, was in the protocol.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: So that if the protocol had stayed in existence Russia would have had the same terms as Canada, so far as lumber is concerned?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The six months' delay is running now, and article 21 really does not come into effect until the termination of that delay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
If my hon. friend suggests that it does not come into effect, I reply that it comes into effect in so far as it is possible to make it effective, because it has been approved and assented to by the British 
parliament. But so far as the ability to operate every section of it is concerned, it would be necessary, as I have said, that the six months should have run before it could operate in its entirety.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Would the Prime
Minister indicate to us a little more clearly and definitely what class of action taken by a foreign state would come under that part of the section which reads:
. . . the creation or maintenance directly or indirectly of prices for such class of commodities through state action . . .
Recently our own government guaranteed the Canadian banks against loss in connection with the transactions of the selling agency for our wheat, which is being sent abroad at less than the cost of production. In that sense we are dumping wheat, the state itself entering into the dumping process. Would action of that kind on the part of a foreign country come under this clause?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
No statement could be
further from the fact than the one just made. Why it should have been made I know not. To suggest that the government is engaged in the wheat business is as far from the fact as it is possible for any statement to be, and I should think the hon. gentleman would know that. Why did he make that statement? Does anyone know? This aims at a condition under which there is state control of the product of industry or agriculture, where the state itself is the moving power with respect to the production and marketing of it. Where the state intervenes in that manner, so as to frustrate the operation of the preference thus granted by Great Britain to Canada,' Great Britain has said that if attention is drawn to it, such action will be taken as will ensure that the state thus offending shall not be able to sell its product in that market. That is what it means. Either government, of course, has the right to call into operation the provisions of the section. Could anything be further from the fact than to assert that there is any relation between that and the guaranteeing of the financial position of an agency that buys and sells wheat without reference to the government? I cannot understand what purpose is served by making that observation.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It is not necessary that I should explain the purpose I have in view in making an observation. But the Prime Minister has not answered the question. My question was this:	If the government of a foreign country should take action

United Kingdom
similar to that recently taken by our government in guaranteeing the banks against loss when they are advancing money for the sale of wheat, would it come under this clause? That, I take it, is indirect action on the part of the state, if it is not direct action. And I take it further that that is virtually a dumping of grain, because it is selling it at less than the cost of production in the country of origin. Whether or not the Prime Minister agrees with that interpretation of the action of this government I am not immediately concerned, but I ask, if some other state, Germany if you like, in subsidizing its grain, should take action along that line would this clause apply against Germany?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Russia.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Yes, or Russia. I
hare no objection to taking Russia as my illustration, but some people here do not like the mention of Russia, so I took Germany instead. Or take Italy if you like; there are a great many people not so frightened about Italy. In Saturday's Ottawa Journal, an eminently respectable paper, and rather inclined to be Conservative, there appeared a report of a recent statement by Sir Arthur Steel-Mait-land, who, I believe, was Minister of Labour in the last Conservative government in Britain and has just returned from a trip to Russia. He said:
I want Britain to trade with Russia because of the great and growing burden of unemployment. ...	.
Our export trade to Russia last year amounted to $35,000,000 at par. It can easily be trebled. It might well be multiplied manifold.
I ask the Prime Minister the definite question whether, if another state takes action along lines similar to that which we have taken in Canada, this clause will apply against that state?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the language of the article is:
This agreement is made on the express condition that, if either government is satisfied that any preferences hereby granted in respect of any particular class of commodities are likely to be frustrated in whole or in part by reason of the creation or maintenance directly or indirectly of prices for such class of commodities through state action on the part of any ' foreign country, that government hereby declares that it will exercise the powers which it now has or will hereafter take to prohibit the entry from such foreign country *directly or indirectly of such commodities into its country for such time as may be necessary to make effective and to maintain the preferences hereby granted by us.
The hypothetical case suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) does not come within those provisions.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
As far as I am concerned I do not want to have the discussion led off into a question of what action this government has taken in regard to wheat. But I do not think the Prime Minister should be too dogmatic about the effect of this government's intervention. I have before me the order in council authorizing the action referred to by the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth). The recital is that there has been marked variation in grain prices in the immediate past; it refers to the uncertainty as to future prices of wheat, and goes on to provide for guarantees in order that the wheat may be sold for cash at present prices. That is not very far from what this paragraph refers to, namely, the maintenance of prices directly or indirectly through state action, not on the part of any foreign country but on the part of this country. I should think, therefore, there might be seme doubt whether if this sort of action were taken by foreign countries to maintain prices it might not be quite possible that this clause would be invoked by us, and we might present to Cheat Britain that situation and ask (hem for redress. I think the Prime Minister is perhaps unduly restricting the possibilities of this section when he declines to agree that the maintenance of prices in this way, or the assistance in the maintenance of prices, might not come within this section.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if there is any understanding as to the procedure to be adopted in connection with this section. That is, how are representations to be made, or what has	to	be shown in	order that	thesection may	be	invoked by,	let us say,	this
government, through a request to Great Britain in respect of action on the part of some foreign government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The only question of procedure that was discussed with the British authorities was that of first giving notice under the provisions of the protocol. Then if occasion necessitated, and the effect of the offering of state controlled products or commodities at a price	that bore no	relation to	themarket was	to	frustrate the	preference,	this
government could give such notice as might be necessary and, on the facts being verified, the British government would take the necessary action to prevent the importation into that country of the commodity so affected.
