Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
But I was getting at
whether the burden is on the Canadian authorities to satisfy the British government with regard to any infraction of this article.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Of course, as the matter has not yet arisen in practice, I can only say this is one more illustration of the intention of the governments, in making a bargain of this kind, to act in the utmost good faith. I can only repeat that if the facts were brought within the four comers of the article, and the attention of the British government were directed to them, they would make such inquiries as might be necessary to satisfy themselves as to the correctness of the position which, the Canadian government asserted, necessitated their taking appropriate action to accomplish the end in view, namely, the prevention of the frustration of the value of the preference to the exporter.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The Prime Minister objects to the citation of hypothetical cases. I mentioned one which was not hypothetical, that of Germany, which bonuses its exports. I believe South Africa does the same thing. Certainly that is direct action on the part of the state which may affect prices. I would ask whether action of that kind on the part of a state would bring it within the terms of this clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I can only say that if that case ever arises it will be considered. It has not been considered yet by the two governments.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Apparently I am
entirely in error with regard to this whole matter. I thought we were entering into a treaty. If we are doing so it seems to me that this document should set forth certain definite principles which must guide the contracting parties in whatever particular circumstances they may find themselves. If the Prime Minister means that there is a particular country or a particular condition against which this article provides and that it does not have general application, that is a new phase of the matter altogether of which the house knows nothing. We have before us a distinct clause. I have not a great knowledge of law, but from what little knowledge I have I would say we have to deal with the meaning of this article which is before us. I think I am putting a perfectly proper question when I ask the Prime Minister if the action of Germany, or of South Africa, or of any other country which bonuses its ex-
ports, brings it within the terms of this particular clause. It is not a question of whether the matter has been considered; it is a question of whether such action would come under this clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has read the clause, as I have; I have read it to the committee. This is a treaty between Great Britain and Canada, not between Great Britain and Germany or South Africa.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It is a treaty that applies to foreign countries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Just permit me to finish. This treaty is between Great Britain and Canada, and it makes certain provisions. If the conditions which are mentioned in this article obtained, suitable action would be taken by Great Britain or by Canada, if it were the converse of the case I have mentioned, for the purpose of prohibiting importations into the country of the commodities so affected. That is all. I decline to give antecedent interpretations; that is an unwise and a wrong thing to do, as no one knows better than the hon. gentleman. We are dealing with actualities and with those I shall continue to deal. I do not propose to give my interpretation on hypothetical questions which, when they become actual cases, in view of surrounding circumstances and facts, may necessitate action being taken along some line different from an interpretation which I might suggest. That brings the whole matter exactly within what was said a few days ago by the foreign secretary in Great Britain; to undertake to deal with oases that do not exist and to place an interpretation upon a bargain made between the United Kingdom and Canada is not my purpose. I do not think it is fair criticism or fair comment or fair inquiry to make at this time with respect to this bargain.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am sorry the Prime Minister does not think it is fair, but we are discussing this article of the agreement and this is our only opportunity of arriving at what the clause really means. If I understand anything at all about the drawing up of agreements, there were certain definite matters under consideration when this article was drafted. If -the Prime Minister is not in a position to interpret the meaning of the article I do not know who would be in that position, because presumably he was there at the time. I -think it is a fair matter of legal interpretation that the men who had something to do with the drafting of a section should be asked

United Kingdom
to interpret its meaning. I repeat I am not giving a hypothetical case; I have asked with regard to a specific condition existing at the present time. I referred to the action which Germany now is taking, and asked whether or not that would bring that country within the terms of this section. If the Prime Minister refuses to answer of course that is his option, I suppose, although it does not seem very fair that when we are considering the article the Prime Minister will not state whether or not Germany comes under this article at the present time.
I would give another illustration. Suppose the Reconstruction Finance Corporation of the United States undertook some direct or indirect action which might encourage the exportation of goods from that- country. I should like to know whether or not, in that case, the United States would come under this article. Perhaps that is a hypothetical case; so far as I know that has not been done as yet, but such action might be taken by the United States. I do not think we should be asked simply to subscribe to this clause in a blind way without having any definite knowledge as to what it really means or in what it may involve this country. I still think my question with regard to Germany is perfectly proper. It is not hypothetical by any stretch of the imagination.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Certainly I do not want to delay the proceedings of the committee, but I think the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in relation to foreign countries might well be applied to empire countries. I quite understand and quite agree with what was sought in the drafting of this clause. When a country operates a business such as state operated lumber camps, the state pays no royalties and no timber dues. When camps are operated in a capitalistic country such as Canada the state takes certain severe tolls in the way of dues from the private operators, and certainly it is not fair competition for a private lumber company in the Dominion of Canada to have to compete with a state operated lumber company, when that private company is paying to the state substantial taxation on the lumber which it cuts off state owned limits. It is quite possible that in the particular case of Russia, commodities have been placed upon world markets by the government simply for the purpose of securing foreign exchange. When such competition as this exists it is unfair to the normal operation of a business within the British Empire, and I can quite see the object of having an opportunity to enter a complaint against that sort of business.
The question, however, goes much further than that, Mr. Chairman. We in Canada have given state aid to agriculture by paying a bonus of five cents a bushel on wheat. We are operating in the British market in competition with Australia, but Australia has an export bonus scheme with regard to butter. The whole principle of bonusing exports of any commodity at all is in my opinion extremely vicious and wrong. Personally I have never subscribed to it, and I do not subscribe to it now. Bolstering up one particular industry at the expense of other industries by means of a bonus may lead to extreme state expenditure which, in the end, may not result in any definite benefit to the state.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: What is the difference between a bonus and a tariff?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: My hon. friend is entering into a controversy on a point which I should be very glad to discuss with him at another time, but that is not the question here. We also have another situation in Canada. We do a good deal of talking about Russia, but in this dominion we operate provincially-owned power enterprises which pay absolutely no taxation to the state, whereas the privately-owned power companies pay substantial revenues to the provinces for the use of water and very heavy taxation to the state and the municipalities in the conduct of their business, both as to percentage of profits and in the form of municipal taxation. Now, if the principle is to be adopted in this legislation we must remember that we have done and may again be doing a considerable export business in electrical energy with the United States, which will be coming into competition with electrical energy generated by the private capital paying taxes in the country in which it is generated. I say therefore that while the purpose of this legislation is to eliminate unfair competition in our trading with Britain on certain commodities, it opens up a very serious field of discussion. As regards the very commodity in which we are at the present time most interested, and in which the Prime Minister no doubt would argue that he is trying to support us, namely, wheat, I think it is pretty generally understood that the North American continent sold a great many million bushels of wheat to Russia. I believe it is also well known that a great deal of Russian wheat has been sold on the Cardiff market.

This aims at a case in
which unfair competition destroys the price.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The words are these:
. . . are likely to be frustrated in whole or in part by reason of the creation or maintenance directly or indirectly of prices . . .
The word "creation" is there to meet a situation where, as pointed out the other day, one country had through its selling agency given a statement that whatever price was quoted it would quote a lower price. My personal view' is that it has no relation whatever, by any stretch of the imagination, to the bonusing of wheat as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Certainly that was not in anyone's mind when the matter was done. But may I point out that this is an agreement between two coimtries; there is not a third country. It has to be worked out by the two of them and not by somebody else, and the very provisions in the agreement that look towards the maintenance of good faith and mutual discussion and negotiations for the purpose of giving effect to it, preclude the possibility of anyone giving any hard and fast interpretation as to what might or might not follow if this wrere something of universal application. It

is not. This is a contract between two parties, and one of the terms of the contract is contained in article 21. It aims at securing fair competition against unfair state competition; that is all.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Since the Prime Minister has admitted that this is aimed primarily at what he calls unfair state competition, I think it is proper that one should object to this parliament pursuing a policy of this kind. I am firmly convinced that in the years to come, indeed in the very near future, the state will more and more be driven to take action which will directly or indirectly affect business. We have, in fact, been doing it for a great many years in a small way and we are being forced now to do it on a larger scale. The only country which apparently has done it on a national scale is Russia. The Prime Minister says that, with regard to other countries, they were not in the minds of the parties who drew the agreement. I presume that everyone will realize from that statement that Russia was very definitely in the minds of those who drew the agreement, and Russia is the only country that has any form of state capitalism. I think we should consider carefully the results of this action. In the first place, we might very easily antagonize a great country that might be one of our best customers. I have again and again urged that we should trade with Russia. That was the policy of the late government in Great Britain. As I read the papers it is only a question of time until a new agreement will be drawn between Great Britain and Russia, so that trade with Russia is not a matter that can simply be regarded as a vague dream or fad of a few people in this country. We missed a great opportunity a year or two ago when we might have taken Russian coal in exchange for some of our agricultural implements. Now it would appear that we may sacrifice any chance of dealing with this great country which has been the first to go into state enterprise on a large scale.
I might take this opportunity to call the attention of the house to an article in the November number of Current History by Sidney Webb, now Lord Passfield. He points out some of the conditions which now prevail in Russia and which I think should afford ground for careful consideration of the whole situation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Is that relevant to the question?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think it is relevant. He said:
In Soviet Russia the aggregate volume of production is increasing year by year.

United Kingdom
That is something We have to consider- whether we regard Russia as a customer of ours or as a rival; because if we fail to enter into arrangements with Russia at the present time we may easily find her our competitor, and if it should prove that state enterprise is more economical than private enterprise, as I believe the hon. member for North Bruce suggested, we might encounter great difficulties in our wheat-producing industry in the near future. To continue:
Soviet Russia has been able, without popular outcry, for the past two years entirely to suspend its unemployment benefit simply because the government can and does find places at trade union rates of wages, either in productive work or in technical training, for every applicant.
There again the question is raised whether that would be unfair competition. We have in this country some 800,000 persons now under relief.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Yes, but the 800,000 are men, women and children.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Yes, and I suppose there are some 750,000 altogether who are unemployed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Oh, nonsense.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

Yes, 750,000 unemployed. Take the figures shown by the census returns, add the proportion which have come in since the figures were compiled, take into consideration the fact that nearly 200,000 young people have entered the labour market since that time, of whom only a very small proportion have been absorbed; take into account the fact that the census figures do not include the young people who had not yet had jobs and so were not out of a job or, on the other hand, those who have been working for themselves but whose business had gone down-* I think if hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to make a careful estimate they will find that my figure of 750,000 is conservative. If we have 750,000 unemployed and should choose to put them at productive work, paying them out of the state treasury, we might then be in a position to export more goods. If so, some will say that that would be guilty of unfair competition. It might be unfair in one sense, but unfair only from the standpoint of those who believe firmly in private enterprise. It certainly would not be unfair to the state or to the people who are unemployed. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) suggests that it would not be unfair to those people who have to pay the taxes. Sidney Webb goes on to say:
Perhaps this may not be unconnected with the curious fact that the Soviet government
(central and local) is this year spending on the education of its far-flung population of

45.000.	000.

speechtext: I do not think this is relevant.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The state of unemployment in Russia does not interest this committee.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am trying to show that there is great difficulty in deciding what is fair and what is unfair competition. I have been pointing out that under state enterprise huge sums may be spent upon education, upon cultural opportunities for the masses and upon a great variety of other things, but when it comes to one particular item which may be produced at a lower cost than under private competition, the sale of that article when exported is considered to be unfair competition. In order to deal intelligently with the whole question you have to consider all the surroundings.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The statistics concerning unemployment in Russia and Great Britain would not seem to cast any light upon this article or be relevant to the question.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think that they do. I should like to read another paragraph from Sidney Webb as follows:
The essential novelty in economic organization which Soviet Russia, alone among nations, has adopted, is that, from one end of industry to the other, no profitmaker puts a finger in the pie, and no rentier levies his tribute in return for allowing the land and capital to be used.
If we must produce at such great cost because of the heavy tribute which private industry levies upon our production, then I submit that there is no great unfairness in a country cutting out the middleman, cutting out the tribute and producing as nearly as possible at cost. Sidney Webb continues:
The object and purpose of Soviet industry is never pecuniary profit for the proprietor, but always to supply the nation with the largest possible output, of the best possible quality. This is the first great difference in industry between Soviet Russia and the rest of the world. The second is that production and distribution is not left to be decided by the whim or caprice of landlords; or by the calculation as to the likelihood of profit by hundreds of thousands of separate capitalists, or by their managers or their bankers; or even by the
10,000	official factory managers on behalf of the state, but is made the subject of a deliberate, nation-wide planning as to what is best, not for any particular citizen or section of citizens but for the whole community, present and future.
1400	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
If that is a fair statement of the situation in Russia it does not seem to me to be possible to say that the goods there produced are produced under unfair conditions. It has been claimed that Russia is dumping these goods at below cost and for that reason is not able to build up her reserves-forced sales, as it were. My last quotation from Sidney Webb is as follows:
Soviet Russia is year by year diverting from consumption by the present generation of consumers, at least a quarter of what its workers are producing, in order that the consumers in future years may reap the benefit in an assured higher standard of life.
That is a much larger proportion given to capital expenditure than prevails in any other country. Russia is putting aside those reserves, she is adding that much to capital, and any country adding to capital at that rate surely cannot be said to be producing its goods under unfair conditions.
It seems to me that we ought not to take action here which would place us in the position of advocating the perpetuation of our system of private competition, under which we are suffering from such tremendous depression at the present time and under which so many of our people are on the verge of starvation, when there is another system being tried out and from which we could derive some knowledge as to how conditions might be improved in this country. I do not defend everything that is being done in Russia, but I do say that an experiment is being worked out there which is worthy of our consideration. We might very well place ourselves in such relationship to Russia that she might send us some of her surplus goods which we need, and that we might in return export some of our capital goods which she needs at the present time. I think such a transaction would be beneficial to both of us. As it is to-day, we are deliberately setting out to make trade war upon any country that proposes to carry on state enterprises to a greater extent than we ourselves, at the present moment, are prepared to undertake.
Article 21 agreed to.
On article 22:
This agreement between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and His Majesty's government in Canada is to be regarded as coming into effect as from the date hereof (subject to the necessary legislative or other action being taken as soon as may be practicable hereafter). It shall remain in force for a period of five years, and if not denounced six months before the end of that period shall continue in force thereafter until a date six months after notice of denuniciation has been given by either party.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think it is
important to repeat what has been said with respect to the effect of this particular article. It differs from most of the articles that usually appear in agreements in that it seeks not only to impose additional taxation but to fix that taxation at a certain level over a period of five years. That, as has frequently been said, is a violation of fundamental principle of the control of the commons over taxation. My right hon. friend has been fond of quoting from time to time the Procedure of the House of Commons by Redlich, and I should like to quote for his benefit as well as that of the committee what Redlich has to say on page 126 of volume 3 of that work under the title of "Fundamental principles" :
With a view to maintaining parliamentary control over taxation from year to year, a constitutional practice has been established whereby at least one important customs duty and at least one important direct tax are made subject to annual renewal. Accordingly, whether the financial arrangements of any given year require the imposition of additional taxation or not, an act must be passed every year to continue these expiring imposts; and when the Finance bill, in which such renewal is proposed, is before the house it is competent for any member to raise the question, not only of the renewal of the particular imposts in question, but of the continuance of any other duty or tax, whatever may be the statutory time limit, if any, prescribed for it.
He goes on to say:
For many years the tea duty and the income tax have for this purpose been imposed year by year for one year only.
And elsewhere he says:
Apart, therefore, from the special cases of the tea duty and the income tax, it may be said that the presence or absence of a specific time limit in the act imposing a duty or tax has little practical importance, except as affording an indication of the intention of parliament at the time it was imposed.
I do not imagine my right hon. friend will take exception to that statement of the position by Redlich. It serves to emphasize how careful the British parliament has been to see that even with respect to duties which it is proposed to have maintained for a period of years, that the commons should assert its right to revise the entire schedule at any time that parliament might desire so to do by bringing up at least one item for discussion every session. Undoubtedly the intention of hon. gentlemen opposite is to have these duties continue for a period of five years. The intention, so far as 'this side of the house is concerned, is to preserve fiscal freedom in the matter of imposition of taxa-

United, Kingdom
tion, whether that be in the form of customs duties or in any other form, and to resist as strongly as we can anything that will seek to make permanent any rate of customs duty or to give rigidity or fixity to the customs schedule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Surely the right hon. gentleman is not serious in what he has been saying.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Why does my right hon. friend say that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I have a high regard for my right hon. friend's intelligence, wide experience and great knowledge, but when he stands in this committee and makes a statement such as he has just made with respect to taxation, I wonder whether he thinks the house has no memory. I wonder whether my right hon. friend realizes, for instance, that the Czechoslovakian treaty is for four years, and it touched every item of imports from that country. The treaty which Cobden made with France was for ten years. Our treaty with the West Indies was for twelve years. Our treaty with France, lasted nine. Similar consideration applied to treaties with Belgium and Italy.
These are the fundamental principles which I think we must remember: First, we have negotiated an agreement with the United Kingdom; second, the agreement is based upon the application of the principle of tariff preferences, free entry being accorded to the British Empire and a tariff being imposed against those who are not within the empire. The preference is the difference between free entry and the duties which run as high as 33i per cent. Then comes the question as to how long this agreement shall endure. A channel of trade thus created can be developed only within a reasonable time, and I suggest to my right hon. friend that he convert his former Minister of Justice before he tries to convert the rest of Canada and the house; for that hon. gentleman made it quite clear the other day that he realized there must be time with respect to the development of a channel of trade and that time is all important. The question how long might well be the subject of differences of opinion, but that there must be a reasonable time is clear. We have fixed it at five years. This is not taxation in the sense in which Redlich is using the term in the citation my right hon. friend made from him, but it is an effort by tariffs to provide for preference to Great Britain and the dominions.
Just one word more need be said, and that is all I shall have to say about the matter.
We believe these principles upon which we are proceeding are sound, and until this debate was precipitated I thought that all parties were desirous of granting these preferences. My right hon. friend says: We do not believe in a certain fixed tenure. If you apply the principle of landlord and tenant, he does not believe in a fixed rent for a certain period. I say that his government did the same thing. This very day I had to consider, because, my attention had been directed to it, the Czechoslovakian treaty, its date of expiry, four years from the day it was made, and what our rights were under it. What is the difference between the right hon. gentleman making a bargain with Czechoslovakia for four years and our making one with our kinsmen for five? That is the real point. I do not desire to be captious, but I do not think any principle is involved. This house was asked to agree and did agree to the right hon. gentleman's suggestion to adopt that treaty with Czechoslovakia and I am merely suggesting a period of five years with Great Britain is not different in principle from a period of four years with Czechoslovakia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
No one knows better than my right hon. friend that there are agreements and agreements, and that the scope, the terms and provisions of an agreement have everything to do with its general acceptability. The intention of parliament is usually made clear during a discussion of these matters. My right hon. friend talks about an agreement with Czechoslovakia, I venture to say that when that agreement was put through, the point that that agreement should not extend for the term of years it was stated it would extend was not so much as raised by the opposition of the day, the simple reason being that the agreement did not attempt to impose additional burdens of taxation on Canada over a period of years. What I wish to make clear at the moment is this: While the government may have one intention in this matter of the customs duties being fixed by this agreement, certainly, so far as the Liberal party is concerned, it has quite an opposite intention with respect to making permanent any increase in customs tariff at this time. It is just as well that should be made quite clear. There is a great difference again between agreements that are made for a period of years but which can be ended at any time upon so many months' notice, or agreements that affect a very small number of items in a customs tariff, and agreements such as the present one which under the guise of an agreement is in reality an upward tariff revision on a large scale. Our opposition to

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
this agreement is that while it purports to be an agreement to further trade between Canada and Great Britain, it is in reality a means of increasing the Canadian customs tariff by a subterfuge, and one which we do not propose to countenance for one minute. It is an attempt to do something in the nature of an innovation in tariff matters which is being very strongly resisted in other free parliaments at the present time and which we intend to resist as long as we can in this, namely, an endeavour to institute permanent or fixed tariffs and that on a very high level.
May I point this out, that never before, so far as I can recall, in the history of this parliament, has an effort been made to do away with the benefits of an intermediate tariff. The tariff policy of Canada has for years contemplated three distinct tariffs, namely, the British preferential tariff at one level, the intermediate at another, and the general at another. The idea has been that through the intermediate tariff Canada would have an opportunity to make agreements with other countries, giving them certain favourable opportunities in our markets when they were prepared to give us like opportunities in theirs. That is now being destroyed by the way in which the present tariff, under schedule E, has been framed. As has been pointed out over and over again in committee, the agreement raises the intermediate tariff to the level of the general tariff, thereby doing away for the next five years with any advantage which might have been offered to a foreign country prepared to make an agreement with Canada. Hon. members on this side of the house are ready and anxious to trade with Great Britain as far as possible. We also desire, however, to trade with the rest of the world. The mere diversion of trade will not help to bring Canada out of a period of depression such as that from which she is now suffering. There will have to be an increase in the volume of trade, and that increase will have to be obtained not only through trade with Great Britain but through trade with the rest of the world as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee further than to repeat a view expressed by Mr. Runciman in the English House of Commons. The right hon. gentleman opposite says: "We desire to trade with Great Britain." If by that he means we desire to have a trade treaty with Great Britain, then he must mean a contract. Every contract with respect to trade imposes some restriction upon the freedom of action of both parties concerned. As Mr. Runciman pointed out, there cannot be a contract be-

tween parties which does not involve some restriction on our free will and general actions. If it is a contract for service, one must carry it out. If it is a contract to sell goods, one cannot sell them to someone else. Restrictions are clear and implied. But this is the point I wish to make: Is a contract for five years bad when one for four years is good? The right hon. gentleman suggests the answer is that the present agreement involves heavy taxation upon the Canadian people. What about the West Indies treaty? That treaty was for twelve years, not five, and imposed a taxation upon the Canadian people of $5,000,000 a year. We cannot relieve ourselves of that treaty, because it is there and we are not free. Why does the right hon. gentleman opposite condemn the treaty now before us when it is only for five years, when as the leader of a former administration he was the author of a treaty with the West Indies for twelve years which cost Canada $5,000,000 a year? The Czechoslovakian treaty, which is set out at page 234 of the consolidated copy of the Customs Tariff and Amendments was made for the purpose of securing certain benefits for Canada which, I am sorry to say, probably through no fault of the government, did not eventuate. Article 6 of the Czechoslovakian agreement states in part, as follows:
It shall come into force fifteen days after the exchange of ratifications and shall be binding upon the contracting parties during four years from the date of its coming into force.
Those are the provisions, and it seems to me under the present circumstances we are not asking too much, having at one time given assent to a treaty with our neighbours in the West Indies for a period of twelve years which involves us, in connection with the commodity of sugar, in taxation to the extent of about $5,000,000 a year, and having at another time entered into an agreement with Czechoslovakia for a treaty for four years-in the light of these facts it does not seem to me that we are asking too much when we ask for concurrence in a contract for five years with our kinsmen across the sea, comprising some 40,000,000 people.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It is true an
agreement was made, as the Prime Minister has said, with our kinsmen in the West Indies. My recollection however is that no exception was taken by him or other hon. gentlemen opposite at the time to the provisions of the agreements and in particular to the time for which it was to run.

speechtext: All parties in the house were in agreement. That is a very different matter from an effort to bind subsequent parliaments on a matter in connection with which there are between the political parties fundamental differences of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
A few minutes ago the
right hon. gentleman opposite said that he objected as a matter of principle.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
There can be no question as to carrying out anything for a term of years where all are in agreement. But, in this House of Commons at the present time there is a very distinct difference of view as to the merits of the agreement. Hon. members opposite think they have done something which is very much in the interests of Canada. Hon. members on this side feel that the agreement they have made will be detrimental to Canada. I believe we shall find that before it has been in force very long conditions which are now very bad will be intensified in virtue of the additional restrictions being placed upon trade by the agreement now before us.
I do not know that there is anything further to add; I think the position of hon. members on this side of the house has been made clear. The Prime Minister spoke about an agreement made by Great Britain with France. As he well knows, that was a treaty to increase freedom of trade not only between France and Great Britain but between all the countries of the world and Great Britain. In that treaty the same opportunities were given to other countries as were given to Great Britain. The agreement now before us seeks to deny to the world at large opportunities of trade and, as the Prime Minister himself has said, to make it necessary for every foreign country to pay tribute to any part of the British empire it wishes to trade with. He has said this is an agreement framed for the purpose of shutting out the foreigner. Certainly that is what it is for, as the text of it well discloses. Hon. members on this side of the house are certainly not going to become parties to an agreement which places on Canada an obligation to shut out other nations from trading with her.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I shall take only a
moment to reply to the right hon. leader of the opposition. I wish to be sure that the house and country clearly understands the principle upheld by him. A treaty for four years between a foreign country and Canada is submitted to this house, a treaty signed, as I observe, by the former Minister of Trade
and Commerce. A treaty between the West Indies and the Dominion of Canada, part of the British Empire, is made for a period of twelve years by gentlemen who are now in the opposition, and approved by the then opposition, now the government. But when the government now in power submits a treaty with the motherland for five years rather than twelve or four, the present opposition, then the government, must oppose it as being bad in principle. We are asked to believe that position is sound. Hon. members opposite suggest that having supported a four year and a twelve year treaty they cannot now support a five year treaty, because we are led to believe that the right hon. gentleman opposite who asked the house to accept the four year and twelve year treaties was wrong, and that therefore this treaty is wrong. You cannot trust an opposition very far, if it is an opposition of that kind, can you?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am not going to allow the Prime Minister to place any such interpretation upon my words. Any one who will read the text of my remarks will see that he has placed an entirely wrong construction upon them. I am quite prepared to leave it at that. As the right hon. gentleman well knows my objection to the length of time for which the government is seeking to bind this country has been in respect to something which, fundamentally, is entirely wrong, namely, a further increase of duties at this time in addition to all the duties which have already been imposed and further an attempt in large part to rivet these higher rates upon the country for the next five years.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The treaties to which my right hon. friend has referred were treaties which provided generous and assured preferences, and as such they were agreed to. I want for a moment, in connection with this article, to point out to the committee just what we have and what we have not in the way of assurance of preferences under this treaty. To what does this five years apply? What preferences do we get, and how many of these are unequivocally and unconditionally guaranteed for five years? First my right hon. friend says that we get free entry of our goods into the British market for five years. Well and good. There is nothing to say that every other country in the world does not get free entry also, except as to the few items to which I will refer. So I think we can leave the free entry out. I do not think my right hon. friend would argue that we have received
1404	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
a great concession on account of getting free entry, in view of the privilege of every other country to get free entry as well.
What else do we get? We get schedule C. Therein are listed six items on which there is a guarantee of unconditional, unequivocal preference for five years. That is to say, Great Britain undertakes that the duties on those six articles shall not be reduced without the consent of the Canadian government. What are those articles? Timber, fish, fresh, sea; salmon, canned; other fish, canned; asbestos; zinc; and lead. Putting them together, what they amount to is, timber, fish, fresh and canned, asbestos, zinc and lead. Now there are five articles. Let us look at these articles for a moment. Zinc and lead must be delivered at world prices before we get the preference-that leaves only timber; fish, fresh and canned; and asbestos, as the three items in this whole treaty as to which we are unconditionally guaranteed a five year preference at a certain rate, and the rate is ten per cent.
My right hon. friend will say: You are forgetting schedule B-

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: What about apples?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
We will deal with that in a moment. Remember this schedule C, which is the only one as to which there is a guarantee that the duties will be kept up, deals only with timber, fish and asbestos, unconditionally; zinc and lead must be delivered to Great Britain at world prices or else the preference will not be allowed. Now what about schedule B? The provision of article 2 is that the government of Great Britain will invite the parliament of Great Britain to impose the duties set out in schedule B. I point out, as has been pointed out before, that there is no provision in this treaty which says that those duties having been imposed will be maintained for five years. On the contrary the provision which purports to fix the duration of duties follows after article 2; it is article 3, and it provides only that the duties in respect of schedule C are to be maintained for five years and says nothing about schedule B. Now what are the articles in schedule B? They are apples, raw and canned, pears, and dried fruits. It is provided that parliament will be invited to impose the duties mentioned in schedule B on these articles. But there are other articles, they are wheat and copper. Are they unconditional? Not a bit. You find that as to wheat and copper, the duties may be removed if they are not delivered at world prices on first sale. What other articles in schedule B? The right hon. Prime Minister

will say dairy products. Let us look and see what the provisions of the agreement are as to those. Butter, cheese, eggs in shell, and condensed milk; he will say the five years applies to those articles. But he forgets schedule A. Schedule A says that those articles, butter, cheese, eggs in shell and condensed milk, need only be admitted free for three years, and that after three years Great Britain may impose duties on those articles so long as she maintains preferential margins; and they are veiy careful to say, not "existing" or "the" preferential margin, but just "preferential margins." The Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other night that he understood that to mean that Britain would maintain the existing preferential margins. If so it is remarkable that they did not say so. You find "existing" margin expressly mentioned in article 7, but not here. As far as the letter of this agreement is concerned- I am going to deal with the spirit in a moment-there is no provision whatever that the British duties on apples, pears and dried fruits shall be maintained against the rest of the world for five years. Secondly there is no provision that British duties on butter, cheese, eggs in shell and condensed milk shall not be imposed against Canada so as practically to wipe out any preference to Canada.
That is the situation. I have dealt with every article there is in that schedule. Now what is the result of it all? After we have got through we find, coming back to what I said first, that there are just three items in this whole schedule, timber, fish and asbestos as to which this five years unconditionally and expressly applies and on which a definite preference, a definite margin of ten per cent for five years is given. And the only three items to which that five years might apply without any condition are apples, raw and canned, pears and dried fruit. Wheat and copper have the condition that they must be sold at world prices. The same with zinc and lead. And butter, cheese, eggs in shell and condensed milk, that is dairy products, all have the provision that at the end of three years the free entry may cease and we may have a duty imposed against us, so that there will be practically no preference at all. That is all there is in this treaty as far as assured preferences are concerned, and that is all to which this five years applies.
But the Prime Minister will suggest that there is something in regard to tobacco, bacon and cattle. As to tobacco, the provision is that Great Britain will maintain a preference on our tobacco as long as she maintains a duty, but she may take the duty off at any

United Kingdom
time. In regard to bacon we know what the arrangement is: if Great Britain puts its house in order, if after the report of the pig commission an arrangement is made in regard to domestic production, if regulations are made then Canada will have 2,500,000 hundredweight of bacon admitted free to Britain. But it is "as, if and when." With regard to cattle the provision says that the arrangement which has already been made-not an arrangement made by this agreement-will be carried out. That is what we get from Great Britain; those are the things for which we make certain concessions.
What are the concessions? I am only going into that for just a moment. We give a fixed preferential margin on 223 tariff items. On 159 of those items we agree that the duty will remain at least as high as it is today for the next five years, because we are giving Great Britain free entry and we are agreeing to maintain the preferential margin, which means we have to keep the duty where it stands or put it higher. On 139 of these items the duty has been increased in order to get the concessions, as my right hon. friend would call them, in connection with this treaty, namely a fixed ten per cent duty on the items to which I have referred, plus the additional concessions which I have enumerated.
My right hon. friend will say we are attempting to cross "t's" and dot "i's," and that it is too strict a construction of this agreement. There has been a good deal of talk during these debates about good faith and about the spirit of the agreement. My right hon. friend used the words "warp and woof"; he said that we would find in the warp and woof of the agreement thus and so. I say to my right hon. friend that the British businessman's word is just as good as his bond; everyone admits that-, but when you have required the bond from him, when you have got him to sign the bond, then he proposes to be bound by what the bond says and the bond is here. So far my right hon. friend has failed to produce a single sentence spoken by any statesman of Great Britain which changes or alters the construction which has been put upon this agreement from this side of the house. So far as we can learn everyone over in Great Britain believes that their tariff can be changed as to our goods going into Great Britain except the few I have mentioned. They believe that they can change the duties on these goods from time to time, if they so desire, and as a matter of fact they propose to change them. Even this tariff with regard to apples, pears and dried fruits can be changed; a newspaper article which was read the other night indicated that Great Britain
considers that she does not have to maintain these duties for five years.
That is the situation, and when we talk about good faith we must remember that the gentlemen who came over here are skilled draftsmen; they met our representatives who are skilled draftsmen also, and together they drafted the agieement. It is not just a friendly letter from one to the other; it is a real, definite, binding document intended to be such, and I have no doubt that many hours were spent over the phrasing of this document. I do not expect that it will lie either in their mouths or in ours to say, "Well, true the agreement says that, but we meant something else." Least of all will it lie in our mouths to say that Great Britain is bound to maintain tariffs against the world in our favour on a general list of goods when the only provision we have required with regard to their maintaining tariffs is contained in clause 3, which has reference only to these six items included in schedule C. On the other hand Great Britain has been just as careful; in article 9 it is definitely provided, in effect, that we cannot reduce the preferential margins given on the goods set out in schedule E, which comprise 223 items. There you have the bargain which we are considering tonight.
I had a good deal of sympathy with the Prime Minister when he suggested that it was hardly fair that he should be asked to interpret this agreement. Why? Because he knows it will be interpreted in accordance with the letter of the agreement; because he knows there will be differences in connection with the interpretation. If it were simply a friendly letter, a memorandum in general terms, then he could have dealt with the spirit of it, but this is the agreement itself. He said to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, "I have read it and you have read it; see what you make out of it." He did not attempt to suggest that there was something else in the atmosphere of the agreement which would assist in its interpretation. The agreement is there, and I think I have put on the record fairly and exactly the effect of that agreement in accordance with the way it is written. So I do not think we should say that we expect the British to live up to this agreement in "good faith" as if there were some understanding outside the agreement itself. They will live up to it in good faith; they will live up to what they have signed, and they will say that what they have signed is this agreement, and no one can blame them for doing so.
Having received these things and having given these other things, what is the result? The result is that during these five years Great Britain can go to Switzerland, if you
1406	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
like, and say, "We want to buy clocks from you." She can go to the United States and say, "We want to buy some of your electrical manufactures, and we will bring down our tariff in order to do so." They may ask, "Yes, but have you not made an agreement with Canada?" Great Britain can reply, "Yes, but we did not agree to maintain a duty against you; we can let in clocks and electrical goods from Switzerland and the United States just as we let them in from Canada." They can deal with Germany in regard to cutlery and with Belgium in regard to glass and glass bottles, to take a few of the items mentioned by the Prime Minister. They can deal with Austria in regard to optical instruments and with the Orient in regard to carpets. They can deal with France in regard to toilet articles, and so on. Their hands are absolutely free; they can go to the world economic conference and say to any countiy, "We will take your goods free," or "we will impose a tariff of five per cent or ten per cent," as the case may be.
What is our position? With regard to 223 items our position is that we can make no bargain whatever with any other countries which will interfere with the margin of preference to Britain. This is the difference between the agreement now before us and other trade treaties, to which my right hon. leader has referred. We must say to any other country, "We cannot make any agreement with regard to these items; our tariff is fixed for the next five years. Britain is free; our hands are tied. Let us take our lumbermen when they go to sell their products. The other night my right hon. friend the Prime Minister intimated that this ten per cent preference would help the lumber business of Canada. I wish it would, but I am afraid that as against Finnish lumber, because of the exchange situation, our lumber will not get into the British market. Why are we looking for a market in Great Britain? The Prime Minister told us that formerly we sent
1,446,000,000 feet of lumber to the United States, and what did he say about our market in that country? He said that because of the United States import tax of $3 per thousand that market was practically closed to Canada. Why is it closed? Because of the tariff which my right hon. friend put on in 1930 and 1931, the red-blooded tariff which was talked about by the Minister of Railways. That led to the United States putting a duty of $3 per thousand and another duty of $1 per thousand against our lumber. The result is that we are frantically scurrying around looking for a market in which we can sell our lumber.
[Mr. Ralston.1

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: There is nothing to that at all.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
No, I suppose there is
no relation between the two circumstances except that they happened to about synchronize. We put on the duty against the United States, and immediately the United States came back at us with a duty of $3 and SI per thousand feet, and as a result we are looking for a market for 1,446,000,000 feet of lumber. Does my right hon. friend believe a ten per cent preference is going to find a market for that amount of lumber? According to the figures he gave us the most we ever sold to Great Britain under normal conditions was 186,000,000 feet, yet he expects that we are going to be able to market this vast quantity of Canadian lumber under a ten per cent preference. The same thing applies to fish. The Prime Minister said the United States market was closed to us; he said, "The United States high tariff makes wider markets elsewhere imperative". That United States high tariff is due in no small part to the tariff attitude of this government taken in 1930 and 1931. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance knows that the United States has been seriously considering imposing a duty on our live lobsters because of the attitude we take towards that country.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Oh, I know my hon.
friends do not want to be responsible for their acts at all. They rvant to be able to shut out the foreigner; they want to close the door against the world and still be able to sell our goods everywhere. I say that cannot be done, and that is all there is to it.
That is the situation, Mr. Chairman, and that brings out the real difficulty facing us. We have tied our hands. We have lost the goodwill of good customers all over this globe. We are going to find it difficult to sell our wheat in competition with the man from the Argentine. He can go to the man in Europe and say, "Are you going to buy wheat from Canada? That is the country where they are shutting out the foreigner. We will give you a run for your money, but you cannot get Canada to take any commodities in exchange for their wheat. They are shutting out foreign products." With regard to our paper and wood products we must face competition in the United States market from Scandinavia. They will be able to tell their customers that we are the people who want to shut out

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
foreign produets. The same thing applies to cattle, to furs and to minerals. Here are two important objections to this agreement. In the first place it ties our hands completely in regard to any arrangements we might wish to make in order to sell our goods. In the second plaoe it leaves a bad taste in the mouths of our customers and loses to us their goodwill.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the analysis I have made of the schedules contained in this treaty indicates that this five year provision means that we do all the giving for five years and get very little in the way of benefits. As my right hon. leader has said, we have used the United Kingdom agreement in order to tie ourselves definitely to a tariff higher than we ever had before, at the same time closing the markets of the world to us because we insist on closing our markets to the products of other countries.
