speakerposition: topic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire as a member of this house to direct attention to certain grievances and to ask redress from the government. We have now been in session about seven weeks, discussing important matters arising out of the Imperial economic conference. It is not my wish in any way to belittle the importance of that conference or to dispute the value of the agreements that have been arrived at and the discussion that has taken place thereon, but I do believe that there is at the present time something that is of far greater importance to this country, something that is agitating the minds of the people of Canada to a greater degree now than even these agreements which have been under consideration from the 6th day of October to the present moment.
We are going through a very severe economic crisis, the effects of which are being felt by all sections of the community, and in my opinion the house would better serve the interests of the people by discussing the economic conditions that prevail in this country than by engaging in such discussions as we have had during the past few weeks. In the course of the debate this evening the question of unemployment arose and figures were submitted to the house by my hon. colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), who made the statement that in Canada at this moment there are about three-quarters of a million persons out of work. From that statement there was a certain amount of dissent. I have attempted to analyse the figures given to the house recently by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) from the census returns and by every ordinary mathematical calculation I have made to arrive at the number of persons unemployed in Canada today, I have reached approximately the same figure as stated by my colleague. In view of the fact that some hon. members seem to dispute the figures given by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, perhaps it might be well for me to suggest the method I have followed in my computation.
It is stated in the census returns that as at June 1, 1931, there were 392,809 persons unem-
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

ployed in Canada. That was the total number. In addition to that, there was a temporary army of unemployed of 42,443, making a grand total of 435,252. Now, if that was the total as at June 1, 1931, how are we to arrive at the unemployment figure today? This is the way in which I arrived at the present figure. If I take the employment index figure as at September 1, 1929, which was the peak of employment in Canada, I find that it was 126-8, and on June 1, 1931, the index figure was down to 103-6. That meant, by percentages, that there was a reduction in employment in that period of approximately 18 per cent. If 18 per cent represents the difference between the index figures on September 1, 1929, and June 1, 1931, the question is, how shall we arrive at the figure at the present time? About September 1, 1929, there may have been out of work in Canada approximately 35,252 persons, and if at that time there were that number out of work, then there has been an increase of 400,000 between that date in 1929 and June 1, 1931. Now, between June 1, 1931, and October 1, 1932, the index figure of employment has dropped to 86-7, which means a further reduction of 16 per cent. If 18 per cent represents 400,000 unemployed, then an additional reduction of 16 per cent would bring the total number of unemployed to approximately 750,000.
I am not stating these figures in order to make capital out of them but simply in order that we may have the facts clearly before us; it will then be easier for us to adopt a more intelligent attitude towards this question than has been adopted for a number of years past.
I hope the party flavour will not be permitted to enter into this discussion. When oa-rty passions rise we are apt to lose sight x the importance of the matter under consideration, and at times we indulge in the sport of one party getting after the other. This is probably the most serious unemployment situation ever faced by this country, and I hope hon. gentlemen will not forget the vast number of unemployed and those who are dependent upon them.
As I have stated, the unemployed number about 750,000. The census figures show an employable total of 2,500,000, so it would appear that more than twenty-five per cent of our total employable population is without employment. If we discuss the past, I hope we will discuss it in such a way as to be a guide to our future actions. If we learn from experience, we should be better equipped to guide ourselves in what we may do for the 
future. There have been many discussions in this house in the past upon unemployment. Going back to 1925, when I was first elected to this house, I cannot remember a session when I did not raise this problem in one way or another. Therefore, I do not feel that I need to apologize, especially under present conditions, for raising this question and asking redress from the government.
It has been stated in some quarters that this problem is of a temporary character. But it has been confronting us ever since the crash and debacle of 1929; from that time onward things have been going from bad to worse until today we have reached a situation where no one can predict what will happen in the immediate future. When a condition such as this has prevailed for about three years, I do not think anyone will be bold enough to say it is temporary in character. Prosperity has been promised to us for many years, but it seems to be as far away as ever. We have been told it is "just around the corner," that we have "reached the bottom," that there are "signs of a revival," but I do not think these statements are taken seriously now by many people in the dominion.
The government has attempted to deal with this problem; only the other day the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), informed the house that there were 800,000 souls being fed by the government. That is a stupendous number, about eight per cent of our total population, yet it does not take into consideration those who are being looked after through other sources. The old manner of dealing with the unemployment problem apparently has proved to be inadequate. We have failed to find a solution of the problem; we have failed to improve conditions, and I think it is about time we looked in other directions for relief. As one branch of parliament we have great responsibilities which cannot be overlooked, even though some would like to overlook them. The people of this country are looking to parliament for redress; they have elected us as members of the House of Commons in the hope that we may be able to improve conditions. I have no doubt that every hon. member of this house said something about unemployment when he stood for election a little over two years ago. He promised he would try to bring about better and improved conditions for those whom he hoped to represent in this house. If the unemployed of this country cannot look to parliament for redress, I wonder in which direction they will look? In my humble opinion this parliament is the only place where the vast masses of our people

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
can look to for redress at the present time. We were sent to this house by the votes of human beings, we are here to represent human beings more than we are here to represent property rights or property interests. When we deal with questions so important as unemployment, the human element should receive our first consideration.
As a nation I believe we are today wealthier than ever before in our history, yet, paradoxical as it may seem, in this year 1932, the more bread we have, the more breadlines there are; the more shoes we produce, the more shoeless there are; the more clothes we manufacture, the more there are without clothes; the more homes we build, the more there are looking for shelter; the more wealth we produce, the greater is the poverty. If such conditions exist, then it is up to parliament to study these problems, perhaps from a different angle than that from which they have been studied in the past, and discuss them in the light of newer methods than have been adopted in the past in Canada and other parts of the world.
I think the people of this generation have more understanding. They have a little more education than our fathers or those who have gone before us, and they see the things to which I have just referred. They see this tremendous abundance accompanied by great poverty. This unemployment problem is one which this parliament ought not to attempt to shelve; it is a problem which should be dealt with and this parliament should not adjourn until it has been dealt with.
Even with this tremendous accumulation of wealth and commodities, because of the lack of opportunity to the average person in this country to have access to this consumable wealth, our workshops are more or less at a standstill and men and women in large numbers are out of employment. Not only are there large numbers out of employment but there are hundreds of thousands of people who are today working short time and earning hardly sufficient to keep body and soul together. We have idle men, idle women and idle factories as well as a tremendous amount of consumable goods lying idle in our warehouses. It would appear that industry and finance under their private ownership have failed completely to function and have been responsible for bringing about the present crisis. I think it is the duty of parliament to attempt at least to find a way out of the difficulties which confront us. The financial debacle of recent year's has not affected our wealth one iota. It is quite true that paper fortunes have disappeared; that people who a few years ago thought they
were wealthy find today that they may not be as wealthy as they thought they were; but that does not mean that the real wealth of the country has disappeared from our midst. The real wealth of the country lies in our factories, workshops, warehouses and natural resources. It is only when those natural resources have applied to them the labour power of the people that real wealth is produced, and today we have that in abundance. We have more up-to-date equipment in our factories than we have ever had before in our history, but at the present time, as a result of the chaotic conditions through which we are passing, we are not producing anything for the benefit of the great masses of the people.
I might cite as an example of what I have just stated to the house a case which occurs to my mind. I refer to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I am citing that, not because I have anything in particular against that institution, but because it comes to my mind at the moment. A few years ago the shares of that company reached a value of something like $250 each, and at that time the people who owned them thought they possessed a great deal of wealth. Those shares have dropped to about S60-I am speaking approximately-and those who thought they were wealthy found the largest part of their wealth had disappeared; what they thought was worth S250 is worth today only about $60. No real wealth however has disappeared; the only thing that disappeared was the value oi those shares, and it did so because the. railway was not utilized to the same extent as it was in previous years and is not able to pay the dividends it formerly did. But in spite of the fact that the shares may be only a quarter of what they were previously, the whole of the rolling stock, equipment, roadbed, hotels, steamships, are here today exactly as they were a few years ago. What applies to the Canadian Pacific applies to practically every other industrial concern in the dominion. What has disappeared, to a very large extent, is values, but the wealth of the country is present today-in probably greater abundance -than it has ever been before in our history.
If our industries are not functioning-and we know they are not-one of the duties of parliament should be at least to attempt to see that they function and that the men who were formerly employed in them are again employed and given an opportunity of earning a decent livelihood. For many years all these industries which have been under private ownership and control have to a certain degree been able to accumulate profits; they have
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

continued to operate as long as profits were in sight, but the moment profits are not available, those industries naturally cease to function. Then the question immediately occurs to my mind: What should be the purpose of industry? In my opinion the purpose of industry should be primarily to satisfy the wants of the human beings within the community. But such is not the case. Today the primary purpose of industry is not to supply the needs of the human beings in the community, but to see that those who own the industries reap their rewards and profit from them.
There is no doubt that at the present time we are facing an acute economic crisis. This is not the first time in the history of Canada that we have faced a crisis. My mind goes back to the time of the war when we were facing a very severe external crisis, and when the government of the day mobilized, so far as it could, the man power of the country and found that under the circumstances it had the right to call upon human beings to give their lives, if need be, in coming to the rescue of the state. If in a time of crisis the life of a human being is not too sacred for the government to lay hands upon, I think we can at least afford to take courageous action in the present circumstances, and even if we go to the extent of doing something which might impair property rights, we would be quite justified in taking such steps. I believe the present emergency is in many respects even greater than that of 1914. We have today not an external crisis, but an internal one where three-quarters of a million people find themselves without employment and, what is even worse, without any prospect in the immediate future of their being absorbed into any kind of industry. I want the house for a moment to attempt to realize what that means-three-quarters of a million people, men and women, tramping the streets day in and day out, week in and week out, looking for a job when there is no job, and then perhaps after a time, against their will, being compelled to seek public assistance in order to keep body and soul together 1 I know many of those men who are out of work; I know the difficulty and the tremendous ordeal it must be for them, probably for the first time in their lives, to be compelled to go to a public body and ask for assistance. The first time it is done with extreme reluctance; the second time is not so hard as the first; the third is not so hard as the second and the fourth is even easier than the third. Finally they reach a stage where we ourselves, as a result of our inaction in this internal crisis, have de-
moralized perhaps hundreds of thousands of our own people. I should like to impress upon the house the seriousness of that aspect of the situation-hundreds of thousands of people in this dominion, so rich in its resources and wealth, with no hope or prospect of being able to accomplish anything in the immediate future in the way of earning their own livelihood.
We have been told many a time in this house about the courage and fortitude of our Canadian people. I wish a little courage could be shown in this house and that we would take courageous action in order to meet the existing crisis. Parliament has a duty; it also has certain functions. I believe the first function of parliament is to govern, and the second is to see that our people are fed, clothed and sheltered. I am not going to say how the latter function is to be fulfilled, but I believe these are two of the main functions of government. The state is supposed to be the guardian of public rights and public wellbeing. If we at this juncture in our history admit our impotence to deal with the present economic situation, then this is an admission of our total unfitness and inability to govern. Parliament in its supremacy has allowed institutions to grow up that are more powerful than parliament itself. It is high time that parliament, having over a period of years allowed those institutions to grow up and become as powerful as they are today, should re-assert its supremacy and be what it ought to be, the sovereign body in the land.
During the past fifteen or twenty years production in Canada as well as in other parts of the world has increased by leaps and bounds. One would have thought that with the enormous increase in production during the last fifteen or twenty years there would have been increased happiness and increased contentment among the great masses of people. Unfortunately that has not been so. Increased production has merely meant an increased spread between wages and production, and the benefit of it has gone to comparatively few people in Canada.
For a few moments I should like to direct my remarks to production, consumption and wages. Statistics show that during the past few years the average production of a person in employment has increased approximately 50 per cent; in other words every person working in industries over a period of fifteen years has shown an increase in his productive capacity or efficiency of approximately fifty per cent. During that same period wages have increased comparatively little, and the whole advantage from increased productivity has

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
gone to comparatively few people. It has also been shown that wages today in relation to production are only about twenty-five per cent; in other words, I think our statistics show that a person receiving $1,000 per year in wages is producing $4,000 worth of commodities. I claim therefore that unless that spread between wages and production is narrowed down, made much smaller than it is, there is no hope of solving the problem of unemployment, because the money received by a person in wages represents his purchasing power. If he can buy back only one-quarter of that which he produces there is bound to be an accumulation of commodities which will not be consumed, and the greater the accumulation the greater ultimately is the problem of unemployment.
When I refer to production and wages, and say that I ivant to narrow down the spread, I do not wish hon. members to think that I would narrow it down by reducing production. First of all, I wish to see real wages increased. Secondly, I wish to see production kept at a high level, because I still believe the more capital goods we can produce, the more consumable goods we can produce, the better it should be for all concerned. I do say, however, that there ought to be a reasonable level between production and consumption, otherwise we shall continue to be faced with problems with which we are confronted today. I do not wish to cut down production; far from it. I want to increase consumption. Some people in recent months have advocated cutting down production. I am opposed to cutting down in any way our productive capacity; on the contrary I should prefer to begin at the other end of the problem and make an effort to increase the consumptive opportunities of the Canadian people. Therefore when I speak of balanced production, or reasonably balanced production and consumption, I imply an opportunity to increase our consumption to an extent much greater than obtains at the present time.
At this point I am pleased to observe that in recent weeks the Prime Minister himself has been discussing the matter from a very different angle than usual. It would seem that recently his views are changed from those he held in past years. I note that on November 4 the right hon. gentleman spoke in the city of Montreal and discussed briefly the problem of unemployment. The heading in the Montread Star is as follows:
Accusations answered in fighting speech here.
Then follow the Prime Minister's remarks:
The cataclysm that has struck our civilization is a catastrophe of a universal scale, it has touched every country in the world and the
hundreds of thousands and millions of unemployed that we find in every part of the world are the direct result of overproduction, underdistribution and buying, the lessening of purchasing power and the development of all those tendencies that are attributable to the Great war and its after effects.
I must congratulate the Prime Minister on the great advance he has made, and I hope he will continue to show the same progress in the future as is reflected in his speech delivered in Montreal. However there are some further comments attributed to him about which I am not so enthusiastic. He said:
When that was once realized, we then understood clearly that no action of Canada with its
10,000,000 souls could make any perceptible dint on this terrible catastrophe.
That was also part of the Prime Minister's statement concerning the problem of unemployment, but with this latter assertion I cannot agree. True, we are suffering from a world condition; true, again, people in Canada are no doubt suffering in part, from conditions prevailing in other parts of the world. But if we have in Canada hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat, and if the people in China, Japan or other parts of the world cannot buy our wheat, that is no excuse for people within our own borders being without bread. If we have a surplus of all commodities and people in other parts of the world are unable to consume those commodities, that is no reason why our Canadian people should do without the things produced within the dominion. If other countries cannot buy our goods, at least we should put that purchasing power into the hands of our own people and give them the opportunity to buy the things which we are producing in superabundance.
The crisis through which we are passing has not been visited upon us by some supernatural force. This is a man-made crisis, and if it is man-made, if we are in some degree responsible, I think there should be, and I have no doubt there is, sufficient intelligence among our own people to enable us to get out of it. This government and other governments have made efforts to deal with the unemployment problem. A good many remedies have been tried. The present government has put into effect a great deal of legislation designed to meet an emergent situation. I state frankly that the government has done a great deal by way of direct relief and creating relief works but relief and relief works are not a cure for unemployment.
I do not wish to take up too much time of the house, but I should like to deal with one or two aspects of the question of unemployment. First, there are the men, women and children who are without any visible means
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

of subsistence at the present time, and to whom immediate attention must be given. In connection with them there is a necessity for direct relief pure and simple. For their comfort the government have done a great deal, but its activities have been purely administrative. If the amount of relief is not sufficient-and many people say it is not- then we are faced with a question of administrative action to raise the amount of relief sufficient to meet the needs of the unemployed. At the moment, however, I am more deeply concerned with the problem of unemployment than in the relief of the unemployed. I think I am not limited, Mr. Speaker, to forty minutes on this occasion, as I intend to move an amendment which will perhaps give me the extra time that I desire. A few moments ago I said I wanted the house to take courageous aetion on this question of unemployment. I know the amendment I am about to move will not at first sight look so very courageous, 'but I think that before we take action we should at least have more information before us, and under the circumstances I would hardly expect the whole house to sit and discuss in detail this very important question. Therefore I think it desirable to have a committee or commission go into this question of unemployment in the most thorough way possible, and my amendment will deal with the question of the appointment of such a committee or commission. Then I will deal with what I should like to be the terms of reference to such body. I therefore move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted:
That in the opinion of this house it is desirable that a committee or commission be appointed to consider the economic situation in the dominion with special reference to unemployment and to report back during the present session of parliament.
I have said that in dealing with this unemployment question we have tried the method of relief, we have tried public works, and neither of these has been found to be a remedy for the situation. We have tried tariffs, and tariffs have not solved the problem. We have tried reductions in wages, and that has only accentuated the problem. We have tried dismissing men and women from employment, and our lead was followed by a great many other people, but that again has only aggravated the problem and in no way tended towards a solution. In Great Britain, where they are faced with a somewhat similar situation, they thought a year or so ago that their solution lay in remaining on the gold standard. Then when they went off the gold

standard they thought that by doing so their problem would be solved. But neither remaining on nor going off the gold standard has proved to be a solution. In view of all the efforts made in this parliament and in other countries, I think it is obvious that there is something radically wrong with the whole of our economic structure, that the conditions which have existed for three years will not yield to the methods which have been adopted by this and other governments. Therefore I claim that it is the duty of this- parliament to attempt to find a way out of the difficulty. Many men and women today are expressing keen dissatisfaction with the existing order of things. They feel that perhaps we have to look for a new social order to provide the way out. For these reasons I ask that this matter be referred to a committee or commission for investigation.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: What is your suggestion for the cure of unemployment?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend has heard
me speak in this house on many occasions and I have put forward many a time my own *method of dealing with this question. If I had not moved this amendment I would have been very happy to deal more exhaustively with what I would suggest as a way out. In putting my amendment, which is seconded by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) I would like to refer to that committee or commission eight items which I suggest should be the terms of reference.
First, I would like it to consider ways and means of eliminating unemployment-a rather tall order, I admit. Second, I would like it to consider the question of jurisdiction as between federal and provincial governments; third, seasonal unemployment; fourth, technological unemployment; fifth, reduction of hours of labour; sixth, increase of real wages; seventh, annual productive capacity and consumption in relation thereto, and also the potential productive capacity of the Dominion, of Canada; and eighth, the spread between wages and production.
I do not know whether at any previous time this House of Commons has ever appointed a committee or commission to consider questions of the kind to which I have just referred. I know that in 1919 a commission was appointed by this parliament that dealt with the internal unrest. They made an exhaustive investigation, lasting approximately two months. From the time the order in council was passed until that commission reported back to parliament less than three

Unemployment-Mr. Bennett
months' time was consumed. In their report they said that the chief causes of unrest were, first, unemployment and the fear of unemployment. That was away back in 1919. Later in the report they recommended an immediate inquiry into the question of state insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. During all the intervening period of about thirteen and a half years this parliament outside of the couple of years that we inquired into the question of unemployment insurance, and the promise which the right hon. Prime Minister made to introduce legislation during the life of this parliament dealing with the question-and I hope that promise will be carried out in the near future-except for that we have done nothing fundamental with the unemployment problem, and today we are faced with the most serious problem that we have erver been faced with in the history of Canada. Therefore I think it is time this parliament took action.
I know it may be said by some that this is a provincial question. But I do not think so, because already this parliament has footed a very large part of the unemployment costs. I know that in the election of 1930, as well as on previous occasions, unemployment was the chief issue, and it was that on which the people of this country voted as they did in 1930. Now we have to go back to our con-situeneies when this parliament adjourns in the next week or so, and face our constituents. We have got to face people who are out of work. I know that when I go back to my own constituency, or almost any constituency in Canada, and address the people on questions of the hour, the first question that is always put to me is: What is parliament doing about economic conditions? What is parliament doing about the unemployment situation? So far this session what could I tell them? We have done practically nothing. We have been in session six or seven weeks and up to now have not discussed in any fundamental or even ordinary way the question of unemployment. Therefore I would ask the house to give to my amendment that consideration which I believe it deserves. I have not put it before the house with the idea of attempting to shelve the question of unemployment, I would like the government to understand that. I have asked that the committee or commission deal with this question immediately and in a fundamental way, because I believe that if they do that, they would be bound to come back with some fundamental suggestions to deal with the problem, which so far we have not faced in the w'ay it ought to be faced.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the people of this country together with the people in other parts of the world are going through a very difficult period. In other countries we see governments tottering, we see upheavals, we see men and women hungry and appealing in one way or another for the chance to earn a decent, honest livelihood. For many years the great masses of the people in this country, as well as those in other parts of the world, put up a stern fight for what we might term a political democracy, for the right to vote and have their own representatives in parliament to express their opinions. That fight has been won; it is almost history today. Now there is another fight to be won; we are entering upon another phase of civilization. Today it is a question not of a political democracy but of an industrial democracy in which the great masses of the people of this country will have the opportunity to enjoy the fruits of their labour, to work and help build up a state worth while, a state in which every ablebodied man and woman can do something, in his or her own way, for the good of the country, which will look upon the individual as a part of the state and give to him an opportunity of working and living in decency, comfort and happiness. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will accept the suggestions I have made and start to deal with this very important question in a fundamental way.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
I rise merely to direct attention to a
rule that has been observed in this parliament since we have had a parliament. I refer to the rule that a matter debated and disposed of should not be raised again during the same session. Rightly or wrongly the matter was presented in an amendment to the address, moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition, in these words:
Whilst reserving any expression of view upon the merits of the agreements concluded at the recent Imperial economic conference, this house is of the opinion that the tariff policies of the present administration have seriously injured the trade of Canada . . .
Then later:
The house regrets that, except the dole, the government has no policy with respect to the relief of unemployment.
That will be found at pages 80 and 81 of the votes and proceedings. Then a subamendment was moved in which the currency question was under consideration, and it was alleged that the effect of the changes recommended by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), would be to provide employ-
Unemployment-Point oj Order

ment for our people. That was the substance of the subamendment. On those motions the house divided; on the subamendment the vote was 18 to 66, and on the amendment 30 to 60.
There is no more salutary rule than that once the debate is concluded and the vote taken, the same question shall not be again raised during the same session. The matter was debated at very considerable length on the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition, and it was competent to those who now have moved this amendment to have moved a subamendment, because in either event the motion is one of want of confidence. May also lays down the rule that inasmuch as in the estimates there is an amount of $976,000 in this connection, the motion is out of order.
But whether you invoke the first or the second rule, the one thing clear is that opportunity for discussion has been offered. That opportunity w'as availed of, with the result that the amendment and the subamendment to which I have referred were negatived. The government has no objection to the fullest possible discussion of any question, within the rules, on going into committee of ways and means or supply, but it is another thing altogether when a motion of want of confidence is raised in this manner. Therefore I regard it as my duty to direct attention to the fact that the rules of the house do not contemplate more than one debate on the same matter during the same session, involving in either case a motion of want of confidence in the administration.

But unless it was

It was discussed on the

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, my submission is that the motion made by my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) is entirely different from the substance of either the amendment moved by my right hon. leader on November 4, or the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod. Both the amendment and the subamendment dealt with the failure of government policy in regard to the unemployment situation, but as I understand the amendment now being moved it is an entirely new matter. It asks that a committee or commission be set up to investigate the economic situation in regard to unemployment and has nothing whatever to say in regard to government policy or lack of policy. It is an entirely new matter that has not been discussed in the house this session, and therefore is entirely in order.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
I will not repeat what my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has just said, but I wanted to raise the same argument. I refer your honour to page 330 of Bourinot, to show that even if the present amendment were part of a former motion it would be in order. On the question of the renewal of a question during a session Bourinot says:
If a motion has been negatived, it cannot be afterwards proposed in the shape of an amendment. In case a motion has been withdrawn it may be again proposed, as the house has not previously determined the question, and it is only in the latter event that the same question may not be revived. If an amendment has been negatived, a similar amendment cannot be proposed on a future day. It has been decided, however, in the Canadian Commons, that an amendment is in order when it comprises only a part and not the whole of a resolution previously voted on by the house.

Unemployment*-Point oj Order
This is not even a part of the amendment moved to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I submit that the point of order is not well taken.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
There is one aspect of the objection which has been raised by the Prime Minister which should not be disregarded. The Prime Minister says in effect that this is a motion of want of confidence. Not having May or Bourmot at hand I must rely on my memory, which I think is pretty good. It will be seen, both in May and Bourinot, that a motion in amendment to a motion to go into supply or into committee of ways and means is not of necessity a motion of want of confidence. More than that, I was a witness myself to the government accepting an amendment to that effect, if the wording of the amendment and the spirit of it were not in condemnation of the government's policy.
Now, the basic difference between the motion made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg and that part of the motion made by the leader of the opposition in the debate on the address is this. Reference to unemployment in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition was a condemnation of the government for their neglect; this is a suggestion which bears no signification of blame whatever. Therefore the government is at liberty either to accept or to reject it. Suppose the government in their wisdom found that the working of such a commission would help them; by accepting this suggestion they would be doing what Mr. Fielding did on one occasion which I related to this house a few weeks ago, the occasion upon which a friend of the government, Mr. Russell, the member for Halifax, offered a suggestion the effect of which was to induce the government to change their policy.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: That happened in connection with the Australian treaty.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
Yes. I remember also another occasion when Mr. Costigan-I think it was he-made a motion which came very near condemning the government; nevertheless it was accepted by Sir John Macdonald because the government found in it some suggestion which they thought might be useful to them.
I respectfully submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Prime Minister that the basic difference between the present motion and the motion which was made by the leader of the opposition lies in the fact that this suggestion is not by way of condemnation of the government, but is rather advice to parliament to adopt a certain measure. I think that for the future, as well as in this instance, the Prime Minister would be well advised to withdraw at least that part of his objection to the motion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: May I mention to the Prime Minister that when the government of the day was considering the reciprocity agreement with the United States, or to proposed changes of the tariff in relation thereto, the house was about to be moved into committee of ways and means, and the Hon. Mr. Monk at the time introduced an amendment which was accepted by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. And that was an amendment not altogether different in spirit from the one which has just been made; is was declaratory of certain rights of the commons in one or two particulars, and it was accepted by the government of the day. The government was about to consider tariff items, just as we are at this very moment, and I think that precedent is a complete answer to what my right hon. friend has said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: I hardly think a government could accept the present motion as anything but a motion of want of confidence. The motion is a tacit condemnation of the government. It calls for a committee to do something which the government has not seen fit to do and therefore, as I say, it is a tacit condemnation of the policy of the government, and as such is a vote of want of confidence which must be resisted. Now, the question of unemployment has actually been discussed and voted upon during the present session. That is the main, thing to consider. The subject has been under discussion and a vote of this chamber has been taken in regard to it. That, Mr. Speaker, rules further discussion, either by way of this amendment or by any other motion, out of order during the present session. The other point raised by the Prime Minister is one which is worth considering too. This whole matter will be under discussion on the estimates; there is an item for unemployment in the estimates. Surely there is some termination to discussions in this parliament.

speechtext: May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that it would be quite possible, under the interpretation which the Prime Minister has attempted to give to the rules of procedure, and in accordance with what the Minister of Justice has said, to shut off discussion of this very item at any time during this session. It would make the speech from the throne comprehensive enough to embrace every question, and the speech having been voted upon no question discussed thereunder might be brought up again. There is no one in this house, may I say, who has availed himself more freely in the past of this very opportunity which I am now seeking than the Prime Minister. I have in my hand Hansard 1930-

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: The question now before the house, Mr. Speaker, is a question of order.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT PROPOSED COMMITTEE OR COMMISSION TO CONSIDER ECONOMIC SITUATION

I am dealing with the question of order. In 1930, I remember, a similar motion was made and was discussed, and there was no question as to the propriety of the motion, after the speech from the throne had been voted upon and an amendment somewhat similar to the one now before us had been discussed. On the motion to go into supply an amendment was moved dealing with unemployment. I will read the amendment to show the difference between the motion made two years ago and the motion now before the house. That motion read:
That all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following he substituted:
"in the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment."
I was glad to observe on March 31, 1930, that the present Prime Minister voted for that amendment. I submit that if the interpretation which the right hon. gentleman now endeavours to put upon the rules of procedure is accepted it will narrow discussion to the point where private members will have practically no redress whatever.
The Minister of Justice has referred to the item in the estimates dealing with unemployment. May I read the item, which appears under administration of justice. There are the following headings: penitentiaries, legislation, agriculture, pensions, mail subsidies and steamship subventions, miscellaneous. Then:
Pensions and National Health-unemployment relief-further amount required, $975,000.

It is for unemployment relief only so far as pensioners are concerned, and when we are in committee on that item the Chairman may quite possibly confine the discussion to that one particular aspect of the unemployment situation. We have not yet reached that item in the estimates, but if the interpretation which the Minister of Justice puts upon the rule is sustained, when the general estimates come before the house it will be impossible to raise any question that is not strictly relevant to that particular item. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that on this occasion, as custodian of the rights of private members, you will come to our assistance and rule the amendment in order.

- My colleague has discussed the extent to which unemployment has grown in this country. I do not think anyone can doubt the seriousness of the situation. . The census figures:as at'June 1, 1931, show 471,668 unemployed, but this figure may have included some who were unemployed through sickness. However, I submit that it does not include those who were working for themselves or those who never had. jobs. There must also be added the large numbers of young people who have not as yet been absorbed into industry. I submit that there is no prospect of improvement in the immediate future. The indices of business conditions are not favourable. It is true the Prime Minister as a professional optimist, along with Mr.-Hoover, another professional optimist, may. tell us that everything is on the mend, but that viewpoint is not borne out by a careful study of business indices. I think we are safe in assuming that there is no sign of relief upon the horizon; indeed the primary causes of unemployment would seem to be permanent. I should like to call the attention of the house to a very suggestive article which appears in the New Outlook of November, 1932. This is an article by Wayne W. Parrish and is entitled "What is Technocracy?" Since there are certain hon. members who do not read these articles upon the economic situation, I propose to read a few extracts. The first is:
. The ancient miller of Athens or Rome ground out in a day, between his two crude milling stones, a barrel to a barrel and a half of indifferent (lour. A modern flour mill in Minneapolis produces 30,000 barrels a day per man with a much shorter day and a much better flour. But for whom?
A shoemaker of ancient Rome took five and a half days to make a pair of shoes. The 7,200 shoemakers in the shoemakers' guild of Roman days would make only 7,200 pairs of shoes in five and a half days. The same number of employees in a modern shoe plant in five and a half days would produce 595,000 pairs of shoes. But for whom?
The brickmalcers for over five thousand years never attained . on the average more than 450 bricks a day per man,-a day being over ten 53719-90
hours. A modern straightline continuous brick plant will produce over 400,000 bricks a day per man. . . .
A photograph of a modern steel rolling mill in full operation will show a large plant without' a human being on the floor. . . . Machines were recently installed which produce 2,500 to 2,600 cigarettes a minute, compared with the previous maximum of 500 to 60.0 cigarettes a minute. . . . A still more fantastic illustration is in incandescent lamp manufacture, where one man is doing today in one hour as much as it took him 9,000 hours to do only so short a time past as 1914. It required only a force of thirty-seven men six weeks to build this high-speed machine.: ... In pig 'iron production one man working one hour can do what it took him 650 hours to, accomplish fifty years ago. In agriculture one man can do in one hour what it required 3,000 hours for him to accomplish in 1S40. A still more striking example is a Milwaukee plant with its daily output capacity of 10.000 automobile chassis frames and 34 miles of pipe line with a total of 208 men in the plant. . . . Technocracy tells us that with what is known now about the application of technology, the adult population of this nation would have to work only four hours a day for four days a week to supply us with all our material needs.
If the statement of these technicians is at all correct, it is manifest that our present way of dealing with unemployment is nonsensical and that we must find some fundamental solution of this problem. I quote again:
The steam engine was introduced, electric power came into being; and within one hundred years we have multiplied the original output rate of the first, or human, engine by 9,000,000, as expressed in. a modern energy transversion unit! But most significant of all is the astounding fact that most of this advance, or 8.766,000 of the 9,000,000 increase, has come within the last thirty years. Is it any wonder that our ancient political system is hopelessly incompetent to furnish the rigorous and exacting technical control necessary to save our highly powered industrial system from collapse?. . . It is after sober, scientific review of such facts that our engineers report that we are faced with the threat of national bankruptcy and perhaps general chaos within eighteen months. .	. .We have been attempting to
operate the delicate controls of a high-powered energy civilization with methods that were crude enough in the ox-cart days when almost every home was self-sufficient and independent. . . . We are faced with the problem of having to desert a system that has become obsolete and at the same time of designing a system to take its place.
I submit that the present relief policy is wholly inadequate, resulting as it does in hardship and demoralization. I thank you. The question is: What can be done? I should like to enumerate briefly some things that can be done. First, the Canadian people can be decently fed, clothed and housed, and no government has any claim upon the loyalty of the people that does not provide at least that for them. Second, I would say that socially necessary work may be provided. The Prime Minister should come back to his original idea and provide for people work at which they can earn wages and thus be enabled to live. Third, the hours can be reduced without reducing wages. That may cause laughter in seme quarters. Unless wages are maintained at the old scale, it would be useless from an economic standpoint to reduce the hours; it would simply mean a few more people would be put to work and the economic situation would not be helped. But I submit that if 750,000 people, or practically a quarter of the people engaged in gainful occupations in this country, are out of work, the work should be spread around. I know some will say that industry cannot stand this and I am quite willing to admit that industry as now constituted cannot stand it. Then I would say that industry must be put upon another basis. I am quite convinced that industry today cannot at the same time provide dividends and also decent living wages, and under those conditions we must consider the possibility of the reorganization of industry.
The next question may readily come:	How
finance any such arrangement as I have suggested? I admit that that is a difficult thing for any government, because I believe again we have arrived at the position where we cannot at the same time pay the interest on our debts and give services. That is the dilemma

Unemployment-Speaker's Ruling
which faces almost every government today. We cannot at the same time pay interest on our indebtedness and give the services needed by the people. This government seems determined that whatever else happens we must pay interest on our bonded indebtedness. I would point out that in England they are adopting a process of conversion under which they are securing money in some cases for less than three per cent. The interest on our national debt is somewhere about $125,000,000 and the interest on the Canadian National debt is $57,000,000, or a total of about $182,000,000. If this were cut in two, it would give us some $90,000,000, and why should it not be cut in two? If the wages of the people are having to be cut; if large numbers are going without work at all; if very large numbers even of our business men have their incomes more than cut in two, I cannot see why those who have accumulated large fortunes ought not to have their incomes cut down by reducing the interest which they receive on their bonds. My colleague spoke of the conscription of men at the time of a national crisis. I cannot see why at the time of this national crisis we should not conscript wealth.
I am not very keen, I may confess, on the amendment as offered by my colleague. I think it has certain advantages in that it would call public attention to this problem not merely during the time of one sitting of parliament but during the whole of the sittings of the commission, and for that reason I was willing to second it. But, after all, what we want at the present time is not so much further investigation, further consideration, as action. We have had consideration for years and years. The Prime Minister told us at the time of the taking of the last census he would have to wait until the results of the census were published before he could bring down an employment scheme. The results of the census are now made public and there is no reason why we cannot act upon those at this session of parliament. I recognize there is a good deal of truth in what my colleague said, that we should have a full investigation of the whole situation, but no investigation can be final in a condition such as that in which we find ourselves today. The world has never before faced such a crisis as is upon us; and I believe all the economists, technicians and financial experts might be brought before that commission and yet at the end of the investigation we would not be very much further ahead than we were at the start. That is my only objection to the setting up of a commission, but anything that will bring the matter before the public I favour. I would 53719-90a
have thought the government would be well advised to adopt this resolution; it would have been advisable politically to do so, because this would have given them a chance to place a certain responsibility upon the commission. But they have turned it down; they have even tried to prevent us from discussing the matter at this time. Under these circumstances the only thing for us to do is to hold the government responsible for immediate action.
